World.title: UBA strengthens Africa’s future leadership pipeline, graduates 374 young professionals
World.content:
Africa’s Global Bank, United Bank for Africa (UBA) Plc, has graduated and inducted 374 young professionals into its workforce, marking the completion of Cohort 21 of its Graduate Management Accelerator Programme (GMAP), the Bank’s flagship talent development scheme.

The ceremony, which was held at Landmark Events Centre in Lagos on Thursday, 20 August, 2025, celebrated graduates from Nigeria and across African countries where the bank operates.

The GMAP programme is designed to equip young professionals with the skills and knowledge needed to navigate and succeed in the banking sector, and has now graduated more than 5,000 young professionals, providing them with the mentorship, training and hands-on experience needed to boost their careers.

The cohort, made up of 223 women and 151 men, was drawn from UBA operations across eight African countries, with 345 graduates from UBA Nigeria and 29 from subsidiaries in Guinea, Tanzania, Kenya, Mozambique, Uganda, Zambia and Côte d’Ivoire.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

UBA’s Group Chairman, Tony Elumelu, who welcomed the graduates, took the opportunity to reinforce customer service as the Bank’s defining edge. Responding to a question on what would set UBA apart as technology makes banking products increasingly similar, he pointed to service as the one advantage competitors cannot copy.

“Products can be commoditised, but service never can, because there is always a differentiator in how you serve and how you create,” Elumelu said. “As everyone leverages technology, the differentiator becomes how that technology is used to make our customers happy.”

Continuing, Elumelu said, “As future leaders of UBA, people like you give me confidence that if we hand over to your generation, UBA will be safe. He also encouraged the cohort to protect their passion and pursue hard work, discipline and excellence throughout their careers.

UBA’s Group Managing Director/CEO, Oliver Alawuba, who took time to congratulate the new intakes, described the certificate they received as a commissioning rather than a conclusion, and urged them to carry the Bank’s standards into every posting.

“You came from different countries, with different experiences and disciplines, but today you have graduated as one UBA family, united by one ambition, to build Africa’s future,” Alawuba said. “Your first posting may not be your preferred destination, but make it your platform and give it your best. No assignment is too small to reveal a great attitude, and no role is too modest for excellence.”

He charged them to learn faster than the world changes, to treat trust as their most valuable asset, and to convert potential into performance, linking each to the Bank’s core values of excellence, enterprise and execution.

The Graduate Management Accelerator Programme is UBA’s structured entry pathway for young graduates, combining technical banking knowledge with practical training in areas such as product design, trade finance and customer experience. The programme forms part of a broader commitment to talent development across the Group, preparing a new generation of bankers to lead the institution and contribute to Africa’s growth.

United Bank for Africa is one of Africa’s largest financial institutions, with more than 45 million customers globally. Operating in 20 African countries, as well as the United Kingdom, the United States, France and the United Arab Emirates, UBA provides retail, commercial and institutional banking services while championing financial inclusion through innovative technology and customer-focused solutions.

World.title: Nigerian actors gather in prayer for Ogogo as he battles stage four cancer
World.content:
No fewer than a hundred star actors on Friday gathered at the BOS Hall (Babajide Olushola Sanwo-Olu Hall), LTV 8, Agidingbi, Ikeja, Lagos, to pray for their ailing colleague, Taiwo “Ogogo” Hassan.

PREMIUM TIMES earlier reported that Ogogo was diagnosed with stage-four cancer and was receiving treatment in a hospital. His daughters, Kira and Haleemah, appealed to Nigerians to help explore further medical options, including traditional treatment, following an alleged refusal by the hospital to treat him.

The prayer session, which was ongoing as of the time of filing this report, came days after some of Ogogo’s colleagues appealed to people who had offered to treat him through traditional and other means not to take offence over their inability to move him from his current hospital.

According to his colleagues, the actor could not be moved from the hospital despite receiving hundreds of offers of medical assistance.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

Those currently at the gathering include the National President of the Theatre Arts and Motion Pictures Practitioners Association of Nigeria (TAMPAN), Bolaji “Mr Latin” Amusan; Jide Kosoko, Yinka Quadri, Fausat Balogun, Antar Laniyan, Bukky Wright, and Yomi Fash-Lanso.

Others include Hassanat Akinwande, Lateef Adedimeji, Toyosi Adesanya and Yemi Ayebo, alongside several other prominent figures in the Yoruba film industry.

Islamic clerics leading the session urged the attendees to pray for Ogogo’s recovery and presented their requests during the prayer.

One of the clerics prayed for healing to reach Ogogo wherever he is receiving treatment and for him to recover from the illness.

Backstory

The prayer session came after Ogogo’s colleagues rallied around him after his daughters revealed that he was battling stage-four cancer and could not travel abroad to seek treatment.

The actors appealed to Nigerians to help the family identify medical specialists and hospitals with the expertise and facilities needed to treat the actor. They stressed that the family was not seeking financial assistance.

According to the actors, Ogogo required specialised medical care, and they urged anyone with information about a qualified specialist or suitable healthcare facility to contact his family.

His daughters also expressed fears about losing their father, saying they were desperate to secure the appropriate treatment for him as quickly as possible.

They disclosed that doctors diagnosed Ogogo with cancer about three weeks earlier and said the actor remained determined to survive. The daughters added that he had repeatedly expressed his desire to live.

World.title: Why Atiku changed his stance on fuel subsidy – Spokesperson
World.content:
The media adviser to former Vice President Atiku Abubakar, Paul Ibe, has defended his principal’s decision to change his position on petrol subsidy, saying a leader should be willing to review a policy when its implementation causes hardship to citizens.

Mr Ibe made the position known in a statement posted on his X handle on Friday, in response to the presidency’s criticism of Atiku’s recent promise to restore petrol subsidy if elected president in 2027.

The Special Adviser to President Bola Tinubu on Information and Strategy, Bayo Onanuga, had criticised Atiku’s position as a reversal of the policy stance he held during the 2023 presidential campaign.

PREMIUM TIMES reported that Atiku, the presidential candidate of the African Democratic Congress (ADC) for the 2027 election, had said he would restore petrol subsidy if elected, arguing that the removal of the subsidy had imposed severe economic pressure on Nigerians without sufficient evidence that the savings had been properly deployed.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

“If I win the presidential election, I will restore the subsidy. And anyone who stole Nigeria’s subsidy funds must return the money,” Atiku said during a Facebook Live session.

He also questioned what had happened to the money saved from ending the subsidy, asking whether the funds had been used to improve healthcare, education and security.

The former vice president acknowledged that he had initially supported the removal of the subsidy but argued that circumstances and the policy’s consequences had changed his position.

His proposal has since triggered a renewed confrontation with the presidency, which accused him of abandoning his earlier economic position for political reasons.

Mr Onanuga argued that returning to a subsidy regime would be retrogressive and fiscally unsustainable, while also challenging Atiku to explain how the proposed subsidy would be funded.

The presidency also disputed Atiku’s claim that the government had accumulated about N30 trillion in savings from subsidy removal, saying there was no such windfall. It argued that the former subsidy system had placed a significant burden on the Nigerian National Petroleum Company Limited and that the removal had helped correct longstanding distortions in the petroleum market.

Leaders must be willing to change course

Responding to the criticism, Mr Ibe said Atiku should not be attacked simply because he was prepared to reconsider a position he held in 2023.

“Leadership and heartlessness should never go together,” he said, arguing that a responsible leader must be prepared to “rethink, restructure or even reverse a policy” where its implementation was causing severe hardship.

Mr Ibe acknowledged that Atiku supported the removal of petrol subsidy during the 2023 campaign, but said changing a policy position after observing its consequences should not automatically be regarded as hypocrisy.

According to him, the more important issue should be whether the policy has improved the lives of ordinary Nigerians and whether the resources released by the reform have translated into better transportation, healthcare, education, employment and social protection.

“Public policy does not work that way,” Mr Ibe said, rejecting the argument that Mr Atiku’s 2023 position should permanently bind him to the policy.

He argued that governments routinely reassess policies, while economists revise assumptions and central banks change course when circumstances change.

“Presidents should be capable of doing the same,” he said.

World Bank data

Mr Ibe also cited World Bank assessments to support his argument that the subsidy removal and other reforms had imposed significant short-term costs on households.

The World Bank said after the subsidy was removed in 2023 that petrol prices increased sharply, with retail gasoline prices rising by an average of 163 per cent. It also said the reform contributed to inflation and placed particular pressure on poor and vulnerable Nigerians.

The bank subsequently maintained that the reforms were necessary to restore fiscal stability but stressed that social protection and compensation would be needed to shield vulnerable households from the effects of higher petrol prices.

More recent World Bank data cited by Mr Ibe showed that an estimated additional seven million Nigerians fell into poverty in 2025, taking the estimated proportion of the population living below the national poverty line to 63 per cent.

The World Bank also said poor households spend up to 70 per cent of their income on food, while noting that improvements in Nigeria’s macroeconomic indicators had not yet translated sufficiently into better living standards for many citizens.

Mr Ibe said the figures underscored the need to assess economic reforms not only by their impact on government finances or macroeconomic indicators but also by their effect on ordinary Nigerians.

He said the distinction should be made between acknowledging the problems associated with the old subsidy system and supporting the manner in which the subsidy was eventually removed.

“There is also an important distinction between recognising that the old subsidy regime was expensive, opaque and vulnerable to abuse and insisting that the only alternative was the manner in which subsidy removal was implemented,” he said.

Atiku’s plan

Mr Ibe said Atiku’s proposed approach was not simply a return to the old subsidy arrangement but part of what he described as the Atiku Economic Recovery Plan (AERP).

He said the plan would focus on reducing domestic refining costs and linking government intervention to locally refined petroleum rather than relying on imported products.

According to him, lower refining costs would translate into lower petrol and diesel prices, which would reduce transportation and logistics expenses across the economy.

READ ALSO: APC accuses Atiku of desperation over pledge to restore fuel subsidy

He said farmers would consequently spend less on transporting agricultural produce to markets, while manufacturers would benefit from lower production and distribution costs.

“Additionally, manufacturers will face lower production and distribution cost,s and businesses will have greater capacity to invest, employ and expand,” he said.

Mr Ibe said the ultimate objective was to revive an economy he claimed had been weakened by the Tinubu administration’s economic policies.

“Ultimately, the Atiku plan will jumpstart the economy laid prostrate by Tinubu’s ‘Bole Kaja’ policies,” he said.

For Mr Ibe, the test of economic policy should ultimately be its effect on Nigerians.

“Policies are made for people. People are not made to suffer indefinitely for policies,” he said, adding that when a policy hurts the population it was designed to serve, “compassionate leadership demands the courage to rethink it.”

World.title: Sokoto Boat Accident: Over 50 bodies recovered, search continues
World.content:
The death toll from the boat accident in Gorau, Goronyo Local Government Area of Sokoto State, has risen above 50 as emergency officials continue to reconcile conflicting figures on the number of passengers, survivors, and those still missing.

Tukur Abubakar, Head of Operations at the National Emergency Management Agency (NEMA) office in Sokoto, said at least 52 bodies had been recovered, according to Daily Trust.

Local sources, however, put the number at 53.

Vanguard reported on Friday that 53 bodies had been recovered after additional victims were brought out of the river.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

Similarly, a local journalist, Sharhabilu Kiliya, told Leadership that residents had buried 46 victims before seven additional bodies were recovered, bringing the number to 53.

The differing figures emerged as NEMA, the Sokoto State Emergency Management Agency (SEMA), the National Inland Waterways Authority (NIWA), security agencies, the Nigerian Red Cross, and local divers continued efforts to establish how many people were aboard the boat.

Mr Abubakar said emergency officials were meeting with other agencies and local authorities to reconcile their records.

SEMA also said officials were still assessing the situation and had yet to establish a definitive number of people affected.

The latest figures are higher than those initially provided to PREMIUM TIMES by the Sokoto State Police Command.

The command’s spokesperson, Ahmad Rufai, told PREMIUM TIMES by telephone on Thursday that 77 passengers were travelling from Gorau to Birjingo when the boat capsized.

He said 46 bodies had been recovered at the time, seven passengers rescued alive, and 24 declared missing.

“There were 77 passengers moving from Gorau to Birjingo. Seven rescued alive and 46 recovered dead, while 24 declared missing. Search is still on,” Mr Rufai said.

NIWA subsequently gave a different account. Its Sokoto Area Manager, Abdulkadir Yusuf, told the News Agency of Nigeria, as reported by Leadership, that the boat was carrying about 82 people, including a community leader, and that 11 people had survived.

Nasiru Adamu, the lawmaker representing Goronyo Constituency in the Sokoto State House of Assembly, also gave a different survivor figure, saying 16 people were rescued.

The discrepancies have made it difficult to determine how many passengers remain unaccounted for.

Aminu Liman Bodinga, Special Adviser to Governor Ahmed Aliyu on SEMA, told Vanguard that emergency agencies were working to determine the actual number of people who boarded the boat.

He said establishing the passenger count was critical to the continuing search operation.

The boat operator and the village head were among those who survived, according to Mr Bodinga.

Survivors recount accident

The village head of Gorau, Aliyu Na-Batsami, told Daily Trust that more than 70 people were aboard the boat, most of them farmers travelling to their farms.

He said children were also among the passengers, most of them girls.

Mr Na-Batsami said the boat capsized in the middle of the waterway and that he managed to stay afloat by holding onto a sack until rescuers reached him.

The newspaper reported that one household lost 11 children in the accident.

Other residents also reported losing several members of their families.

The passengers were predominantly farmers, farm workers, women and children travelling to rice farms across the waterway.

The exact cause of the accident has yet to be formally established.

Mr Adamu, the state lawmaker, attributed the accident to overloading.

He said the boat operator told him that he had tried to stop passengers from overcrowding the vessel, but they refused to heed his warning.

Another resident involved in the rescue operation told Daily Trust that the boat developed a fault shortly after leaving the shore before capsizing.

The accounts have not been independently established as the cause of the accident.

NIWA seeks phase-out of wooden boats

Following the disaster, NIWA Governing Board Chairman Mukhtar Shagari called for stricter adherence to waterway safety measures.

Mr Shagari said NIWA was working towards phasing out wooden boats from Nigeria’s inland waterways as part of efforts to improve passenger safety, according to a statement reported by Vanguard.

He urged boat operators to avoid overloading, early-morning journeys when river tides are high and night travel where poor visibility increases risks.

He also called for stronger collaboration between state governments and NIWA on safety enforcement.

Previous Goronyo accident

The latest accident occurred about a year after another deadly boat mishap in the same local government area.

On 17 August 2025, a canoe carrying more than 50 passengers capsized around Kojiyo village while travelling to Goronyo Market.

Following search and rescue operations, the Sokoto State Government said four passengers died, 41 were rescued, and five remained missing.

The government also announced after the accident that it had procured 20 motorised boats and life jackets for riverine communities, saying two of the boats had been allocated to Goronyo Local Government Area.

In September 2025, the state government formally announced the distribution of 20 motorised boats and 2,000 life jackets to communities dependent on water transportation.

NEMA said Goronyo was among 10 local government areas selected to benefit from the intervention and that boat operators had been trained before the equipment was distributed.

Governor Aliyu warned operators against overloading and directed the chairpersons of the beneficiary local governments to ensure that the boats were properly maintained and secured.

However, Mr Adamu told Daily Trust that following the latest accident, the Gorau community had not received the motorised boats and life jackets distributed by the state government.

It was not immediately clear where the two motorised boats earlier said by the state government to have been allocated to Goronyo were deployed within the local government area, or whether any life jackets from the intervention were assigned to the Gorau crossing point.

Residents have renewed calls for a safer means of crossing the waterway, including the construction of a bridge, noting that farmers regularly cross it to reach their farmland.

World.title: Adeleke’s victory cannot end Accord’s leadership crisis – Factional Chairman
World.content:
The factional National Chairman of the Accord Party, Chris Imumolen, has said the leadership crisis rocking the party is a legal matter that predates Governor Ademola Adeleke’s entry into the party and cannot be resolved by the outcome of the Osun State governorship election.

Mr Imumolen, who spoke at a press conference in Abuja on Friday, said the leadership dispute remained before the courts and would continue despite Mr Adeleke’s victory in the 15 August governorship election.

He said it was, therefore, misleading to portray the internal crisis in Accord as a dispute created by the Osun election or by the governor’s decision to join the party.

“The Osun election is an election. The Accord leadership dispute is a national party and legal matter. They are two different issues,” Mr Imumolen said.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

“The Osun election will come and go. Whichever candidate wins or loses, the national leadership question within Accord remains a matter to be determined through the appropriate legal process.”

Mr Adeleke, the Accord candidate, was declared the winner of the election by the Independent National Electoral Commission (INEC) after polling 511,067 votes, defeating the All Progressives Congress (APC) candidate, Bola Oyebamiji, by 66,252 votes.

However, Mr Imumolen maintained that the electoral victory did not automatically settle the competing claims over who is entitled to lead Accord at the national level.

According to him, the leadership dispute had been in court since 2024 and would continue irrespective of the outcome in Osun.

He said his faction had appealed to the contending sides to resolve the dispute politically but insisted that, having failed to reach an agreement, the courts remained the appropriate avenue for determining the legitimate leadership of the party.

Dispute predates Adeleke

Mr Imumolen rejected suggestions that his faction became a spoiler in Osun because of its opposition to Mr Adeleke.

He said the disagreement within Accord existed before the governor joined the party and that he had previously worked to reconcile the competing factions.

“When I ran, I heard about faction, and the first thing I did was to call the two chairmen. I had a meeting with them, it was televised, and I settled it,” he said.

He was referring to his 2023 presidential campaign on the platform of Accord, during which he said he had succeeded in harmonising the factions.

According to him, the party subsequently operated without the division until its national convention in 2024.

Mr Imumolen said a national convention was held at the Nicon Luxury Hotel in Abuja on 29 July 2024, where two competing claims to the national chairmanship later emerged.

He alleged that members of the faction led by Maxwell Mgbudem left the main venue of the convention and held a separate process in another room, where they allegedly produced their own result.

“We were all at the venue of the convention. The Maxwell Mgbudem faction ran away from the centre where we were having the convention to a room. They took INEC staff to a room where they wrote the result,” he alleged.

Mr Mgbudem’s camp has previously disputed Mr Imumolen’s claim to the national chairmanship, resulting in the competing leadership claims that have continued to generate legal and political disputes within the party.

Mr Imumolen said his faction subsequently went to court to challenge the outcome.

He cited an interim order issued by the High Court of the Federal Capital Territory on 29 August 2024 in Suit No. FCT/HC/M/11850/2024, which, according to him, directed INEC to recognise him as National Chairman pending the determination of the substantive case.

Mr Imumolen said the case had now returned to the Federal High Court and would resume when the court’s vacation ends.

He said his faction would not abandon the case until the courts make a final determination.

“I’m just saying I’m the National Chairman of the party, and I will make sure that the court decides. If the court eventually says I’m not, fine,” he said.

“The court is meant for any one of us to go if we feel we have been cheated to seek redress. That’s what we have done.”

Adeleke’s entry deepened the dispute

Mr Imumolen said the arrival of Mr Adeleke from the Peoples Democratic Party (PDP) to the Accord complicated an already existing leadership problem because, according to him, the governor aligned with one of the contending factions rather than attempting to reconcile the two sides.

Mr Imumolen said he attempted to establish communication with Mr Adeleke after the governor’s entry into the party, but that his efforts did not yield the desired result.

He said former Osun Governor Olagunsoye Oyinlola had contacted him around the period Mr Adeleke was preparing to join Accord.

“I said Governor Oyinlola called me and said, ‘We are coming to Accord.’ I said, ‘Wow, we are waiting,’” he said.

“But after they came, I was calling for three weeks, they did not pick my call.”

He said the disagreement eventually contributed to the emergence of parallel governorship primaries in Osun, with the rival structures producing different candidates.

Mr Imumolen argued that the development should not be interpreted as evidence that his faction was opposed to Accord’s success in Osun.

Rather, he said the faction was seeking to protect what it considered its legitimate political mandate.

“I have no issue with you,” he said, referring to a conversation he claimed to have had with Mr Adeleke.

“I told him, I said I don’t have an issue with you, but I am just here to claim my mandate.”

Accusation of working for APC

The factional chairman also rejected suggestions that his position on the Osun election meant his faction was working for the APC.

His comments followed his faction’s decision, shortly before the election, to withdraw support for Mr Adeleke and endorse Mr Oyebamiji, the APC candidate. The Osun chapter of Accord rejected that position and maintained that Mr Adeleke remained the party’s candidate.

Mr Imumolen said Accord could support different political interests at different levels where it believed such an arrangement served the party’s interests.

He said supporting President Bola Tinubu at the presidential level did not mean Accord would automatically support the APC in every state or election.

“For presidency, the two factions are supporting the APC. Even the governor has also mentioned it, and even myself, we have looked at the president’s policies, his mandate and the rest. We are pleased with it, and we are working with him,” he said.

“But we have candidates who are running for governorship, who are running for other positions in Accord, and we are not, in those positions, working for APC.”

He cited Abia State as another example, saying Accord had supported Governor Alex Otti, a member of the Labour Party, rather than fielding a governorship candidate against him.

Mr Imumolen said such political alignments were part of the discretion available to political parties.

“It depends on how political parties see the direction, and they choose how to move their political trajectory,” he said.

Tinubu support separate from leadership dispute

Mr Imumolen also sought to draw a line between his faction’s position on President Tinubu’s 2027 re-election bid and the ongoing leadership dispute.

He said Accord did not currently have a presidential candidate for the 2027 election because the party had stepped down from the presidential race.

He said his faction would therefore continue to support Mr Tinubu’s re-election while simultaneously pursuing its case against the rival leadership structure.

“There is absolutely no contradiction between supporting President Tinubu and pursuing the Accord leadership case in court,” he said.

“Our presidential position is a political decision. The Accord leadership dispute is a legal and internal party matter. One does not cancel the other.”

He appealed to members and supporters of the party to remain calm and allow the judiciary to determine the competing claims.

“Nobody should attempt to settle the national leadership question through the outcome of the Osun election, political pressure, media propaganda or unilateral declarations,” he said.

World.title: FG inaugurates committees for 67th National Council on Health, demands result-oriented recommendations
World.content:
The Federal Ministry of Health and Social Welfare has inaugurated sub-committees ahead of the 67th Regular National Council on Health (NCH), urging members to ensure that their recommendations are evidence-based, practical and focused on improving healthcare delivery in Nigeria.

The ministry said this on Thursday during the inaugural meeting of the sub-committees in Abuja.

The 67th NCH is scheduled to hold from 16 to 20 November in Lafia, Nasarawa State.

The council, which will bring together key stakeholders across the federal and state health sectors, will be held under the theme, “From Commitment to Results: Delivering Quality and Equitable Healthcare for All Nigerians.”

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

Representing the Permanent Secretary of the ministry, Kachollom Daju, at the meeting, the Director of Health Planning, Research and Statistics, John Ovuoraye, described the NCH as a critical platform for policy dialogue, coordination and decision-making in Nigeria’s health sector.

Daju said the Technical Committee and its subcommittees play an important role in preparing recommendations for the council’s consideration.

“The quality of the work produced by these sub-committees will have a direct bearing on the effectiveness of the recommendations that will be presented to the National Council on Health,” she said.

She urged members to carry out their responsibilities with diligence, integrity, professionalism and objectivity.

Daju also called for an open-minded approach to the assignments and constructive engagement between the Federal Ministry of Health and Social Welfare and the Nasarawa State Local Organising Committee.

According to her, members’ participation reflects a shared commitment to strengthening Nigeria’s health system and improving Nigerians’ health and well-being.

Nasarawa promises collaboration

The Nasarawa State Commissioner for Health, Shekwonugaza Gwamna, represented by the Permanent Secretary of the state Ministry of Health, Ibrahim Hassan, welcomed participants to the meeting.

Mr Hassan reaffirmed the state’s readiness to work with the Federal Ministry of Health and Social Welfare to ensure a successful 67th NCH.

He said the inaugural meeting provided an opportunity for the state’s Local Organising Committee to present the progress made so far, receive guidance from the federal ministry and strengthen preparations for the council.

He thanked members for their commitment and wished them productive deliberations as preparations for the event continue.

Key areas of preparation

The meeting considered several issues relating to preparations for the council, including the formal inauguration of the sub-committees and clarification of the roles and responsibilities of their chairmen and members.

Members also reviewed and worked towards finalising the logo for the 67th NCH, as well as the format and timely submission of memoranda by states.

The meeting was attended physically by officials of the Federal Ministry of Health and Social Welfare, while members of the Nasarawa State Local Organising Committee participated virtually.

The 67th NCH is expected to deliberate on major health priorities and develop actionable recommendations to improve the quality, equity, and responsiveness of healthcare delivery across Nigeria.

World.title: ‘I’m thankful I left US’, Man reveals how mother ‘forced’ him to move to Nigeria
World.content:
File image for illustration.

By Osundiji Sekinat

A Nigerian man, Michael Sonariwo, has recounted how his mother moved him from Atlanta, United States, to Nigeria against his wishes after he completed his sophomore year of high school.

Sonariwo, who was born in Washington, DC, said he moved to Atlanta at the age of three and spent most of his childhood there before his mother decided to return to Nigeria with him and his two younger brothers.

He said the decision came as a shock because he had grown up in Atlanta, attended public school and enjoyed his life there.

“One day after my sophomore year, my mom tells me, ‘Hey, I’m moving to Nigeria.’ And I look at her and I say, ‘Congratulations.’ She looks at me back and says, ‘No, we’re all going,’” Michael recalled.

According to him, he resisted the move throughout the summer, with relatives, friends and members of the Nigerian community in different parts of Atlanta attempting to persuade his mother to allow him to remain in the US.

He said even his pastor offered to let him stay with him, but his mother refused.

Michael eventually agreed to leave after his mother became emotional while driving him home from a farewell sleepover with his friends.

He recalled promising his mother that he would board the flight to Nigeria the following day.

“Once I said I promise, my mom wiped her face, drove back home to Cobb County, packed our stuff, and I was on the Delta flight to Nigeria,” he said.

Sonariwo said he cried throughout the flight to Lagos, prompting a flight attendant to ask his mother if everything was okay.

He claimed that upon arriving in Nigeria, his mother tore up his American passport and enrolled him in a boarding school.

After six months, he said he sneaked out of the school and went with friends to the US Embassy, where he told officials that he was being held against his will.

According to Michael, embassy officials offered him a flight back to the United States, but he declined because he feared being disowned by his family.

He instead remained in Nigeria, where he lived with his grandmother for about two years while his mother settled into the country.

Michael said his experience in Nigeria also came with a major cultural adjustment, particularly after he was enrolled at Supreme Education Foundation (SEF) in Magodo, Lagos.

He recalled being called the “Yankee boy” by classmates because of his strong American accent.

On his first day, he said he struggled to understand some of the school’s disciplinary practices, including being ordered to kneel.

He said the cultural differences eventually led to a confrontation with a teacher, after which he was caned.

Looking back, Sonariwo said the experience helped him adjust to life in Nigeria and understand the importance of parents preparing children for major cultural changes.

He advised parents who plan to send children raised abroad to Nigerian schools, particularly boarding schools, to have conversations with them about the cultural differences they may encounter.

“Make sure you are involved in your children’s life even if you send them to secondary school, especially boarding school, because there are a lot of cultural differences they have to understand,” he said.

Despite initially resenting the move, Sonariwo said he is now grateful that his mother made the decision, saying his life could have taken a different direction had he remained in Atlanta.

He later moved to London for his undergraduate and master’s studies and said his experience of growing up between the United States and Nigeria has shaped his life.
