World.title: Mother of Azerbaijani citizen detained in Russia claims son tortured, forced to speak against Azerbaijan
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, August 21. The mother of Azerbaijani citizen Yadulla Ramiz oglu Rufullayev, who was detained by Russian law enforcement authorities, has said that her son was unjustly detained and subjected to severe torture and psychological pressure by Russian investigators.

Aliya Rufullayeva told Trend that her son had been working as a truck driver to support his three children. She said Russian authorities had brought what she described as fabricated charges against him under Article 276.1 of the Russian Criminal Code (espionage), which she said were not supported by any evidence.

“My son’s truck passed customs control without any problems and was cleared to return to Azerbaijan. However, Russian law enforcement authorities took advantage of the fact that he does not speak Russian and forced him to sign false documents. He has been unlawfully detained for one year and one month. During the investigation, Russian investigators put a bag over his head, taped his mouth shut and tortured him with electric shocks for hours. The Russian side is forcing him to give statements slandering the Azerbaijani state. My son has rejected these unlawful demands by Russian authorities, saying: ‘I would rather spend 20 years in prison than betray my state,’” she said.

The mother noted that Yadulla Rufullayev is the sole breadwinner of the family and that the family is facing difficult social conditions. She also claimed that the state-appointed lawyers provided by the Russian side had acted in a biased and inactive manner.

Another court hearing in the case is expected to take place on August 31.

Official appeals regarding the matter have been submitted to Azerbaijan’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs, the Embassy of Azerbaijan in Russia, the Office of the Ombudsman and other relevant state bodies.

Rufullayeva said her son had faced what she described as arbitrary treatment and discrimination by Russia because he is an Azerbaijani citizen, and appealed for state support to protect his rights and secure his release.

World.title: Washington hosts conference on international academic cooperation (PHOTO)
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, August 21. A conference titled "Connecting Knowledge Beyond Borders: Research and International Academic Cooperation" was held at George Washington University (GW) in the U.S. capital.

The State Committee on Work with Diaspora said the event was organized by the U.S.-Azerbaijan Academic Network and focused on prospects for expanding scientific, academic and institutional cooperation between Azerbaijan and the United States.

Fuad Muradov, chairman of Azerbaijan's State Committee on Work with Diaspora, attended and addressed the conference during his visit to the United States.

"Academic communities play an important role in strengthening ties between countries, expanding the exchange of knowledge and experience, and conveying objective and reliable information about states and peoples to the international community," Muradov said.

He praised cooperation between George Washington University and Azerbaijani universities, noting the importance of academic and scientific ties to the Azerbaijani diaspora's activities. According to Muradov, such partnerships can provide a foundation for joint research projects and long-term academic programs.

He also highlighted various aspects of Azerbaijan's diaspora policy under President Ilham Aliyev.

Sevinc Mammadova, assistant dean for global initiatives at GW's Graduate School of Education and Human Development and a professor, welcomed discussions on relations between Azerbaijan and the United States in academic and scientific circles and thanked the State Committee on Work with Diaspora for supporting the conference.

A panel discussion on academic cooperation was held as part of the conference, bringing together Azerbaijani and international scholars, professors and researchers working at universities across the United States.

The panel was moderated by Turan Waters, director of communications at George Washington University. Speakers included Fuad Muradov; Sevinc Mammadova; Lionel Howard, dean of GW's Graduate School of Education and Human Development and professor of education studies; Matt Winkler, founder of sports management programs at Georgetown University and American University and co-founder and executive director of the SEME Conference; Ali Mammadov, a doctoral researcher in political science at George Mason University and editor-in-chief of the Center for Security Policy Studies; and Can Korman, professor of electrical engineering and associate chair for graduate studies at GW's School of Engineering and Applied Science.

The speakers discussed expanding academic and scientific cooperation between Azerbaijan and the United States, establishing long-term partnerships between universities, developing joint academic research programs, investing in human capital, and exchanging knowledge and expertise. They also considered ways to establish sustainable institutional partnerships.

The participants also exchanged views on the role of the Azerbaijani community in the United States in advancing academic diplomacy and how the knowledge, experience and professional networks of Azerbaijanis abroad could contribute to the development of scientific cooperation between Azerbaijan and the United States.

The panel discussion concluded with a question-and-answer session.

Azerbaijani scholars living in various U.S. states also attended the conference.

The event was described as an important platform for identifying new areas of academic and scientific cooperation between Azerbaijan and the United States, strengthening ties between universities and expanding international academic networks.

World.title: Uzbekistan and Azerbaijan can strengthen Middle Corridor’s role - Uzbek expert (Exclusive)
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, August 21. Uzbekistan and Azerbaijan have significant potential to deepen economic cooperation, while closer integration of their logistics networks could enhance the Middle Corridor’s appeal as a transit route.

This was stated by Uzbek political scientist and Doctor of Political Sciences Saifiddin Juraev in an interview with Trend.

According to the expert, Uzbek-Azerbaijani relations have entered a qualitatively new stage of development, with their potential extending far beyond bilateral trade. “Since the second half of 2016, following Shavkat Mirziyoyev’s election as President of Uzbekistan, bilateral cooperation has undergone a genuine breakthrough. Today, our relations have reached their highest level — that of an alliance — and have taken on an entirely new significance,” Juraev said.

He noted that deeper economic ties should be built around industrial cooperation, energy, the automotive industry, agriculture and investment, while transport connectivity has become the key element linking these sectors. “Trade turnover between the two countries more than tripled in 2025, reaching $795 million. The task for the coming years is to significantly expand economic cooperation,” the expert said.

According to him, one of the most promising directions is moving beyond trade in raw materials and finished goods toward the creation of integrated manufacturing value chains.

He identified energy and petrochemicals as sectors that could become the backbone of this cooperation. “A solid institutional foundation has already been established. This includes the Neftgaztekhnologiya joint venture, operating since 2016, and Turan Energetika APESCO, created by SOCAR and Uzbekneftegaz in 2024, which exports high-pressure polyethylene to Uzbekistan. The new trend is shifting from raw-material trade to joint production of polyethylene, polymers and other gas-chemical products,” Juraev said.

He emphasized that combining the two countries’ industrial strengths creates the basis for export-oriented production networks. “Uzbekistan has growing domestic demand and major gas-chemical facilities, including Shurtan, MTO and GTL projects, while Azerbaijan offers SOCAR’s resource base and access to European markets. Joint petrochemical value chains provide benefits that simple trade cannot — localized value creation, technology transfer and export opportunities in third markets,” he said.

Juraev also highlighted renewable energy as another area with transformative potential, noting that the Green Corridor being developed by Azerbaijan, Kazakhstan and Uzbekistan could elevate energy cooperation to a transregional level. “The Green Corridor project, aimed at exporting renewable electricity across the Caspian Sea, goes far beyond the bilateral agenda. It is linked to European demand for decarbonized electricity and the development of subsea cable infrastructure across the Caspian and onward through the Black Sea. It is a capital-intensive, long-term project, but these are precisely the kinds of initiatives capable of attracting significantly larger volumes of external financing and transforming energy cooperation from bilateral into transregional,” he said.

The expert believes the automotive sector offers similar opportunities. “Chevrolet and Isuzu bus production currently relies largely on semi-knocked-down assembly. The next stage is moving toward component manufacturing and joint exports to third markets, including the Middle East, CIS countries and Iran, using Caspian logistics,” Juraev noted.

He added that Uzbekistan brings a large industrial base and UzAuto’s manufacturing expertise, while Azerbaijan can serve both as a market and as a gateway to international markets.

In agriculture, he said cooperation could expand into food processing, cold-chain logistics, seed production, crop breeding and water-saving technologies. “Both countries are agricultural economies facing similar challenges related to arid farming and water scarcity. In this area, cooperation is complementary rather than competitive,” he said.

According to Juraev, scaling up all of these initiatives ultimately depends on stronger transport infrastructure, particularly the Middle Corridor. “The Middle Corridor’s challenge is not geography but fragmentation: multiple border crossings, Caspian transshipment, different tariff systems, customs procedures and disconnected digital documentation. Transit volumes of 1.4 million tons in 2025, followed by 12.2% growth in the first half of 2026, reflect an upward trend but remain modest by global standards. Turning geography into real transport capacity requires both bilateral and multilateral coordination,” he said.

He argued that the defining concept for the corridor’s next phase should be “synchronization” — aligning tariffs, train schedules, customs procedures and digital documentation along the entire route. “We need through tariffs, one-stop-shop customs mechanisms, coordinated schedules and full digitalization of the corridor. Integrating the logistics systems of Azerbaijan and Uzbekistan systematically enhances the corridor’s attractiveness by making it more predictable in terms of transit times and costs, while giving Central Asian countries more efficient access to global markets,” Juraev said.

He also noted that the Middle Corridor’s growing importance reflects not only its geographic advantages but also the broader diversification of Eurasian logistics. “The rise of the Middle Corridor after 2022 has largely been driven by efforts to reduce dependence on a single Eurasian transport route. Azerbaijan and Uzbekistan are capitalizing on this shift. But the corridor’s long-term resilience will depend not on external circumstances, but on whether it becomes competitive in cost, speed and reliability,” he said.

Juraev identified the China-Kyrgyzstan-Uzbekistan railway as another project capable of reshaping Central Asia’s transport landscape. “Integrating the China-Kyrgyzstan-Uzbekistan railway with the Middle Corridor turns Uzbekistan into a potential consolidation hub. Cargo from China will be able to reach Europe via a shorter southern route through the Caspian Sea, Azerbaijan and other parts of the corridor. For Uzbekistan, which is doubly landlocked, this is strategically significant: Azerbaijan becomes its indispensable western gateway,” he said.

He added that the route through Nakhchivan and Türkiye under the TRIPP framework and the Zangezur direction could become another important component of this system. “Reopening transport links through Nakhchivan to Türkiye would reduce the corridor’s dependence on the single Georgian route and create an alternative overland connection to Europe. Together with the China-Kyrgyzstan-Uzbekistan railway, this could fundamentally reshape the Middle Corridor and strengthen its resilience,” the expert said.

According to Juraev, the development of the corridor is simultaneously laying the groundwork for broader economic integration within the Organization of Turkic States (OTS). “The Middle Corridor is the physical backbone of OTS economic integration, while the Green Corridor represents its energy dimension. Together, the Azerbaijani-Uzbek tandem gives Turkic integration practical substance through transport, energy, trade facilitation and, ultimately, harmonized customs regimes,” he said.

He also pointed to Azerbaijan’s participation in the Consultative Meetings of Central Asian heads of state as another factor creating new opportunities for linking the economies of the two regions. “In effect, a more connected space is emerging — stretching from western China to Anatolia. In this context, Azerbaijan and Uzbekistan can become architects of a new regional framework where transport and energy projects are reinforced by investment and industrial cooperation,” Juraev said.

He added that expanding investment cooperation could further accelerate this process. “The Azerbaijan-Uzbekistan Investment Company, with capital of $500 million, together with the arrival of major investment players, creates a mechanism that reduces risks for private capital. More than 130 companies with Uzbek investment operating in Azerbaijan demonstrate that two-way business engagement is already underway. The next step is to launch large-scale anchor projects capable of connecting investment, manufacturing and logistics,” he said.

In his view, this combination could transform the Middle Corridor into far more than a transport route. “If transport infrastructure moves goods, industrial cooperation and investment ensure that those goods are produced and that value is created. Integrating the Middle Corridor with industrial, energy and investment projects can therefore create not just a transport route, but a fully fledged economic ecosystem linking Central Asia, the Caspian region, the South Caucasus, Türkiye and European markets,” the expert concluded.

World.title: Iranian FM claims new US pressure campaign ‘bound to fail’
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, August 21. Iran’s Foreign Minister rejects new US pressure measures as doomed to fail.

Iranian Foreign Minister Seyed Abbas Araghchi made a post about this on his X social network account today.

“14 years ago: ‘Most crippling sanctions in history.’ Failed.

8 years ago: ‘Maximum pressure.’ Failed.

5 months ago: ‘Unconditional surrender.’ Failed.

Today: ‘Most crushing economic operation ever.’ Bound to fail.

We have seen this movie before. Same bull. Different bullies,” he wrote.

Araghchi stressed that previous attempts to force Iran into submission through sanctions and pressure campaigns have consistently failed, and the latest measures will meet the same fate.

Meanwhile, tensions between Iran and the United States remain high following the months-long conflict that began with US and Israeli airstrikes on February 28. A peace memorandum was signed between the two countries on June 18 under Pakistani mediation, but talks on a final agreement have faced repeated difficulties amid mutual accusations of non-compliance and continued pressure.

World.title: Azerbaijan hosts national championships in acrobatic and aerobic gymnastics (PHOTO)
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, August 21. The 31st Azerbaijan National Championship in acrobatic gymnastics and the 10th National Championship in aerobic gymnastics were held on Aug. 19-20 at the Yardimli Olympic Sports Complex.

The Azerbaijan Gymnastics Federation said gymnasts from various age categories competed for national championship titles.

The acrobatic gymnastics program featured balance, tempo and combined exercises for children, juniors, youth and adults.

Balance and tempo exercises were held on the first day, while combined exercises took place on the second day.

The competitions drew strong interest from spectators in Yardimli. The venue was packed, with large crowds cheering and applauding the gymnasts throughout their performances, creating a lively atmosphere and providing additional motivation for the athletes.

In the women's pairs event among children, the BGM 3 team, comprising Ilaha Ahmadova and Fidan Gurbanova, won gold. The BGM 1 team, comprising Madina Mammadli and Melisa Mammadova, took silver, while the Neftchi 3 team, comprising Madina Bagizada and Daphne Isazade, won bronze.

In the women's groups event among juniors, first place went to the BGM 4 team, comprising Ayan Hajili, Aylin Mammadova and Firuza Gasimzada. The BGM 3 team, comprising Aisha Alicanova, Canan Khalilzada and Zahra Aghaverdiyeva, won silver, while the BGM 1 team, comprising Aziza Aliyeva, Nazrin Hasanovna and Kamilla Tasoyeva, took bronze.

The championship also featured competitions in aerobic gymnastics.

On Aug. 20, athletes competed in individual, trio, mixed pairs and group events in various aerobic gymnastics programs.

In the women's individual event among youth, Ayan Aghayeva won gold, while Fidan Ibrahimova took silver and Amina Mustafayeva won bronze.

Yardimli District Executive Authority head Ayaz Asgarov presented the winners with medals and diplomas at the awards ceremony.

The two-day national championships provided an opportunity for gymnasts to demonstrate their level of preparation, technical skills and teamwork.

World.title: From Hedwig to Bowie, John Cameron Mitchell on art fighting fascism
World.content:
When John Cameron Mitchell first hit the stage in a Farah Fawcett wig at a New York punk rock drag club in the 90s, little did he know he'd be birthing an iconic, transgressive character that would endure more than a quarter-century later.

Hedwig And The Angry Inch began as an off-Broadway musical in 1998, co-written with Stephen Trask and starring Mitchell in the titular role: a genderqueer rock singer from segregated Berlin touring the American Midwest after a botched operation left them with the nominal "angry inch" between their legs.

A 2001 movie written, starring and directed by Mitchell compounded Hedwig's cult status as a lasting "freak flag for the misfit, the outsider", he said.

" That can be anybody, right? … If you didn't feel like you fit in, you understand Hedwig's journey. "

The film's 25th anniversary brings the 63-year-old to Melbourne International Film Festival for a 4K screening with a "stoned or drunk director's commentary", he deadpans.

"Have a nice little edible or a Côtes du Rhône wine," then entertain with insider anecdotes but respectfully not "mess it up" for first-time viewers.

"I'm not interfering with the emotional parts, obviously."

John Cameron Mitchell is a Tony-winning playwright, filmmaker, performer and queer icon. (Supplied: Matthew Placek)

Both the film's subversive humour and nuanced portrayal of love and fluid identity continue to reach and resonate with all kinds of communities: drag, trans, non-binary, film buffs, theatre nerds — you name it.

Not bad for what was initially a box office flop.

Enduring legacy and controversy

After sparking a bidding war among Danny DeVito, Tim Burton and Forest Whitaker, Hedwig's film rights landed with New Line Cinema founder Bob Shaye, who gave Mitchell a $US6 million budget and full creative freedom.

"It couldn't really be mainstreamed," says Mitchell. "It kept it pure. It also meant we didn't make much money because marketing is based on comparing it to something that did make money."

Despite its financial shortcomings, Mitchell says Shaye was "more proud of it in some ways" than New Line's blockbuster Lord of the Rings.

"There's nothing sure-fire about Hedwig commercially." John Cameron Mitchell's film-making debut is now considered a cult and queer classic. (Supplied: MIFF)

Widely screened for free in the wake of the September 11 attacks, Hedwig found new life in the DVD and video market as a word-of-mouth litmus test between friends.

"It was passed around as: 'I think you're gonna like this' or 'If you don't, I may not date you'," explains Mitchell. "I heard that one a lot. And I meet a lot of people with Hedwig tattoos.

" I don't see any Argo tattoos or Gladiator tattoos or whoever else won Best Picture. "

He credits part of Hedwig's lasting effect on the fact "it doesn't smell like Hollywood. It came directly from the depths; the queer rock and roll swamp that was New York in the '90s".

Beneath the glam rock theatre, the film trades in androgynous concepts of "undoing the binarchy", as Mitchell puts it, and timeless storytelling.

"It comes out of Plato. It comes from the Gnostic Christian Gospels. Its origins and its themes are deep, classical, and really useful for people of all genders, of all sexualities, races, ages.

" The audience is never one thing, which is why I always say, anyone can play Hedwig too. "

Some have strongly disagreed.

The Queer Artist Alliance protested a 2020 Sydney Festival staging of Hedwig over the "casting of cis-gender actor Hugh Sheridan", calling it "offensive and damaging to the trans community" in an online letter.

"Not my favourite department of protest, the internet," Mitchell remarks sourly.

"These young, non-binary, internet petition activists decided this is a trans role and must be played by trans actors. And really, they just wanted to play the role."

"And to me, that goes against everything that it stands for."

The would-be Hedwig, Hugh Sheridan. (Supplied: Hedwig and the Angry Inch)

The production was cancelled and Sheridan "tried to kill himself", alleges Mitchell, aggravated at the misunderstanding of a character whose most famous non-trans portrayal, besides himself, is Neil Patrick Harris's Tony Award-winning turn.

Complicating matters was the fact that, privately, Sheridan was "on his own gender journey," says Mitchell. "Who are you to interrupt that?"

In 2021, the Packed To The Rafters actor identified as non-binary and bisexual. In 2024, Sheridan said he was "straight for now" in an interview on The Kyle and Jackie O Show.

For Mitchell, he refuses to have his creation dictated or policed by identity politics.

"It's really about someone recovering from the trauma of people telling them what they are, which is exactly what these petitioners were doing."

"The best communities don't force you into identities. They don't say 'You can't do this because you're gay' or 'You can't write a character that's trans if you're not'.

"I reject that. Fiction is a hallowed institution where we imagine ourselves as people that we are not … If you really want to follow that line of don't tell any story that's not your own, then you might as well cancel all fiction and only have autobiography."

The gospel of Bowie

Punk and rock music has a long history with gender fluidity, "and Hedwig is just one little gemstone on that necklace".

The most influential jewel? David Bowie, a lifelong idol of Mitchell's and an early champion who helped finance a Los Angeles production of Hedwig out of his own pocket.

" He loved [Hedwig]. He told me, 'John, you got it right.' It's the best compliment… "

"But it also implies a certain authority … In other words, he gets to decide. But if you're going to give that authority, you might as well give it to Bowie."

Discussing Bowie produces several fascinating detours.

He shades Lady Gaga as a bad Bowie analogue ("she's just cycling through fashion"). How Australian cabaret artist Meow Meow taught him to crowd-surf in a seated venue (slowly and carefully). Or how his New Orleans artist space features a stained-glass window of Bowie crafted by an Australian living in Canada (shout out Haydn Butler).

Burnt out on Hedwig, one of Mitchell's big regrets was turning down Bowie's offer to adapt Ziggy Stardust for the stage.

"It would have been cool. It was stupid of me to ignore it at the time."

He's made up for it since, staging Bowie-themed productions Queen Bitch, Black Star Symphony and now, I'm Afraid of Americans: A Bowie Song Cycle.

I'm Afraid of Americans provides catharsis with subversive Bowie songs like Sweet Thing, Station To Station, and Big Brother. But also, gentler songs like Heroes, Sorrow and Conversation Piece. (Supplied: John Cameron Mitchell)

Playing Sydney and Melbourne in September, the show sees Mitchell performing Bowie's "most apocalyptic and fascist-facing songs", which became a salve to him after Donald Trump's re-election.

"Let's not even mention the Orange Man," he sighs. "But there's a slow boiling kind of fascism [in America]. People only reading the news they want, which is part of the fascist playbook: You degrade fact and give the facts you want."

He found catharsis in the darker, subversive corners of Bowie's catalogue. "Bowie's never been reassuring. Even his most romantic songs are tense and have fear in them.

"He's not a pure pessimist. He's a realistic romantic in many ways. There is love in there, too. Otherwise, I wouldn't be interested."

Practising punk and what comes next

Mitchell's jam-packed Australian visit also includes presenting a masterclass on punk at the Festival of Dangerous Ideas.

It's an extension of his New York Times opinion piece and 2025 college tour where he instructed younger generations to "stop cancelling each other, find out about punk, and get laid while you're at it".

He believes gen Z should reacquaint themselves with rebellion because their prudish attitudes and politically correct policing, afraid of risks and "internet drunk" on short-form content, have had nasty side effects.

" There would be no fascism in the US without the smartphone, I truly believe that. "

"Because if you're only watching the news you care about, and can't get past 10 seconds of something: Oh look! There's a fascist in charge!"

His Dangerous Ideas presentation will include examples of artists who used art to fight totalitarianism.

Namely, French surrealist Claude Cahun, who fought Nazi-occupied Jersey "in a kind of graffiti, Banksy type way."

Mitchell discovered her "gender-bending art of the 1920s and 30s" in an early 2000s exhibition organised by — you guessed it — Bowie.

John Cameron Mitchell's Australian credentials include directing Nicole Kidman's Oscar-nominated performance in 2010 film Rabbit Hole. (Reuters: Fred Thornhill)

He's writing a new play about Cahun and developing two film biopics on figures who "dealt with their own kinds of fascism."

The first concerns beat poet Alan Ginsberg in 1968, at the height of the Vietnam War and president Richard Nixon's reign.

The other is based upon the "applied punk" of AIDS activist Peter Staley, whose ACT UP coalition successfully pressured big pharma to reduce the astronomic costs of HIV drug AZT. And it sounds like it already has a pivotal scene.

In 1991, Staley had a giant condom placed over the home of senator Jesse Helms in protest of his vehement opposition to funding AIDS research and safe sex practises.

"This horrible, homophobic senator couldn't get out of this big, inflatable condom," Mitchell gushes.

Loading Instagram content

From Hedwig to prophylactic protest, Mitchell is a life-long creator whose work is always interested in interrogating otherness.

"I want things to be not topical, but useful to the moment."

John Cameron Mitchell Presents: Hedwig and the Angry Inch 25th anniversary screens at MIFF on Friday 21 August

Mitchell then appears at Sydney's Festival of Dangerous Ideas on Sunday 23 August.

I'm Afraid Of Americans: A Bowie Song Cycle plays on Sunday 6 September at Sydney's Enmore Theatre and Wednesday 9 September at Melbourne Recital Centre

World.title: From failures to flirtations, Miles Franklin's not-so-brilliant career
World.content:
With the release of Netflix's new TV adaptation of My Brilliant Career last week and the announcement of the winner of this year's Miles Franklin Literary Award earlier this month, August feels like the month of Miles.

Hey, maybe it's the year of Miles, with a recent musical and novel about the writer the latest additions to the growing Miles Franklin canon.

A portrait of Stella Miles Franklin at 21 years old. (Supplied: State Library NSW)

Yet so much of what most people know about the woman who gives her name to not one, but two, of Australia's most prestigious literary awards (the other being the Stella Prize) is limited to what we can draw from her partly biographical debut novel, My Brilliant Career.

That's just her early life and Franklin always insisted the book was less autobiographical than it seemed.

Beyond her gutsy resistance to marriage in favour of her writing career (like her heroine Sybylla), the author's life was filled with failures, flirtations and even a stint under cover.

The 'bush girl' becomes a literary superstar

Stella Maria Sarah Miles Franklin was born in Talbingo, NSW, in 1879, into the squattocracy, and spent the first decade of her life at her family's farm, Brindabella Station.

A depression and drought saw the family (Franklin was the eldest of six siblings) move to shabbier living situations, as did so many farming families at the time.

Stella Miles Franklin, six years old. (Supplied: State Library NSW)

Despite the family's increasingly dire circumstances, Franklin accessed other worlds through books and writing.

By 16, she was writing articles for the local newspaper and working on her first novel, a London-set drama about lords and ladies.

Historian Alecia Simmonds, co-host of ABC podcast The Dead Can't Sue, says: "Literature and writing are the one form of artistic, intellectual, creative expression that women are given [in this period].

" And it is a form of power; it allows them to understand the world, to imagine a new world, and to influence the world — all of which Miles goes on to do. "

Franklin was expected to marry and dedicate herself to housework and children, but instead, Simmonds says, "She really wrote her way out of that destiny".

"Like so many feminists, it [Franklin's desire to write] comes from a collision between the constraints that are placed on women and girls, and the desire for a world beyond those constraints," Alecia Simmonds says. (Supplied: State Library NSW)

After being encouraged by the local newspaper editor to write what she knew, 19-year-old Franklin began work on My Brilliant Career. She wrote it over a six-month period, at night, after her farm chores and sibling minding were done.

In 1899, Franklin wrote to one of the country's biggest publishers, modern-day booksellers Angus & Robertson.

She asked them to kindly read her manuscript and to "state whether or not it is fit for publication". They deemed her manuscript unworthy (a decision George Robertson would later regret).

Miles Franklin's 1899 letter to Angus & Robertson. (Supplied: Harper Collins archives)

Undeterred, Franklin wrote to her literary hero, the bush poet Henry Lawson. With his help, My Brilliant Career was published by British publishers in 1901. Lawson's preface revealed that despite the male pen-name, the author is "just a little bush girl".

It became an international sensation.

"She offers readers a pure bush ideal at a moment of extraordinary turmoil in Australia," Simmonds says. "This is the beginning of Australia's national literary culture."

Miles goes under cover

The success of her debut novel gave Franklin access to the Sydney intelligentsia, and she was befriended by the famous suffragist Rose Scott. Franklin charmed everyone she met, including many men.

"Miles says no to marriage … but she really loves flirting," Simmonds says.

Between 1899 and 1902, she had a flirtation with the other pre-eminent bush poet of her time, Banjo Paterson (of Waltzing Matilda fame). She later said he was "the most sophisticated man that ever attempted to woo me sexually".

Franklin seemed to be on the cusp of a glittering literary career, but her next few books were rejected by publishers.

Perhaps that's because the success of her first book hadn't rescued her from poverty, leaving her with little time to work on her craft.

Miles Franklin (pictured here as a maid) overheard her employers and their guests discussing her book without realising the author was serving them. (Supplied: State Library NSW)

At this point she could've chosen to become a nurse, governess or teacher, but instead, inspired by "girl stunt reporters", she decided to "go under cover" as a maid and servant for wealthy families, taking the name Sarah Frankling, in an effort to investigate the conditions and complaints of the servant class.

"If you are a domestic servant, your day starts at dawn, and this is what Miles writes about," Simmonds says. "They are horrific conditions. You're paid a pittance."

While she was unable to publish her manuscript about her servant experiences over defamation concerns, she began writing for The Sydney Morning Herald.

A broad abroad

With introductions to American feminists facilitated by Scott and Vida Goldstein, and with the hope of getting one in her mounting pile of manuscripts published, Franklin moved to the US in 1906, at 26 years old.

The move led her sister Linda to write to her: "You bad girl, to leave such a lot of broken hearts behind."

By 1907, Franklin was living in Chicago, a bustling city of extreme luxury and poverty, where immigrants toiled in slaughterhouses and sweatshops.

There she worked with social reformer Alice Henry at the National Women's Trade Union League of America.

"Miles is turning up to picket lines," Simmonds explains. "She's there in the rallies. She's running around, collecting strikers' stories and she's witnessing police brutality. She is absolutely in the thick of it."

But it's also in Chicago that Franklin's insomnia and anxiety culminate in a nervous breakdown.

"There is a bush girl in her that just constantly yearns to go home," Simmonds says.

Women delegates to the 1912 Chicago convention of Theodore Roosevelt's Progressive Party. Miles Franklin is second from left. (Supplied: State Library NSW)

Throughout all this, Franklin continued writing and flirting. She became embroiled with two (yes, two) millionaire brothers, one of whom was already married.

"She's politically opposed to marriage, as are many women at this time but … she is open to the idea of marrying [the younger divorced brother]," Simmonds says.

Franklin's biographer Jill Roe alleges the affair ended in 1914 because of an attempted abduction and rape.

After World War I breaks out, Franklin, who was anti-war, moved to England to help on the home front and write about the war effort. She also worked as a cook and orderly at the Scottish Women's Hospital for Serbian soldiers in Macedonia.

Franklin comes home

By 1925, five of Franklin's siblings had died, and she moved back to Australia in 1927.

A year later, Franklin published a pastoral saga under the name Brent of Bin Bin, the first book in a trilogy and her first hit since My Brilliant Career.

In 1931, her father died and her money ran low. But it's also around this time that she returned to her original pen-name, publishing All that Swagger, the novel that restored her reputation in Australia, in 1936.

Franklin began devoting herself towards the very idea of Australian literature itself, championing her peers and local literary journals. She mentored younger writers and used her influence to campaign against censorship.

Hear more about Miles Franklin on ABC's new history podcast Is it appropriate for historians to gossip about the dead? Associate professors Alecia Simmonds and Leigh Boucher aren't afraid to find out.

In 1941, after World War II broke out, Franklin attended a few meetings of the Australia First Movement. The movement was against the war, prioritising Australia over a European conflict, but this ultranationalism slipped into fascist and Nazi territory.

Franklin's friend and publisher Percy Stephensen was one of the movement's leaders.

"But [her biographer Roe contends] that she clearly opposed the views of the movement around Nazism," Simmonds explains. "And she claimed to have not seen the antisemitism until a friend from overseas points it out."

Simmonds suggests it's not straightforward; Franklin attended more than one Australia First meeting and continued to subscribe to the movement's magazine.

"Miles also writes to a friend and says, 'This movement is very much needed,'" Simmonds says.

Franklin, like many 20th century feminists and thinkers, held eugenicist ideas.

The Dead Can't Sue's Leigh Boucher suggests Franklin "is a complicated, complex thinker in a period of intense political and ideological contest and contradiction".

Mother Miles?

In 1946, Franklin finally published the sequel to My Brilliant Career: My Career Goes Bung.

By this stage, she was celebrated as a founding matriarch of Australia's national literary tradition.

But Simmonds says that obscures the legacy of other Australian women writers of her time, including Ada Cambridge, Rosa Praed, Barbara Baynton and Mary Fortune.

"There's no one mother … she's part of this groundswell of women writers."

Miles Franklin's ashes were scattered close to Talbingo, her grandmother's grand estate where she had been born. (Supplied: State Library NSW)

Franklin died in 1954, at age 74. She had published somewhere between 14 and 19 books (depending on whether you count edited collections) under all her various pen-names, but none ever reached the fame of her first.

The Miles Franklin Literary Award, Australia's most prestigious literary prize, exists today because she left her estate, valued at £8,922 (just over $200,000 in today's terms), to establish an award for Australian literature. Nobody knew she'd been squirrelling that money away by living frugally.

Simmonds says, beyond her writing, she'd like Franklin to be remembered as "a social justice activist, feminist, nationalist and an internationalist and this great big, fabulous flirt".

This article is based on research by Alecia Simmonds

World.title: Australia has a soft spot for the amazing flannel flower
World.content:
With soft woolly (and sometimes feathery) star-shaped flowers and grey-green foliage, the flannel flower is a well-known wildflower.

But this beautiful flower has a few superpowers up its floral sleeve.

Out of a group of 10 incredible native flowering plants, the flannel flower has been crowned Australia's most amazing wildflower for National Science Week 2026.

Flannel flowers might look a daisy but they're actually in the Apiaceae family, which includes carrots, celery, parsley, fennel, coriander and cumin. They even have a carroty smell when they are cut.

While most of us are familiar with the beautiful east coast flannel flower Actinotus helianthi — you'll find it in florists and nurseries — there are actually 14 species found in Australia, and one in New Zealand.

The two most common species in Western Australia are Actinotus leucocephalus with creamy white flower heads; and Actinotus superbus, known for its prominent, showy white flowers.

The delightfully feathery Actinotus leucocephalus, one of Western Australia's flannel flowers. (iNaturalist: Hugo Innes, CC BY 4.0)

In the NT, Actinotus schwarzii, is found only on the cliffs of Standley Chasm, says Cathy Offord, head of Australian PlantBank research at the Australian Botanic Gardens.

Tasmania has the tiny crimson flannel flower (Actinotus suffocatus).

The small crimson flannel flower (Actinotus suffocatus) is found only in Tasmania. (iNaturalist: Nick Fitzgerald, CC BY-NC 4.0)

Hope from the ashes

After the devastating 2020 Black Summer bushfires, pink flannel flower (Actinotus forsythii) bloomed across eastern NSW in places they hadn't been seen in decades.

The flowers literally rose from the ashes in their billions in a symbol of hope and resilience.

A bloom of pink flannel flowers on a sandstone plateau on the east coast of NSW. (iNaturalist: Casey, CC BY-NC 4.0)

Dr Offord says the flowers will last for between three to 15 years.

"Mass flowering events produce billions of plants and then over the next couple of years they just fade away."

The pink flannel flower Actinotus forsythii blooming following bushfires. (iNaturalist, waterworks90, CC BY-NC 4.0)

Several other flannel flower species, including two from Western Australia, are known to bloom en masse within a year or two of bushfire.

"One to two years after fire you'll just see a carpet of these flowers," says Dani Hamilton of Kings Park and Botanic Gardens in Perth.

"It's quite breathtaking,"

Seeds have the power of dormancy

Flannel flower seeds can survive for decades in the soil in a dormant state, a trick that explains the plant's ability to suddenly pop up in places it hasn't been seen for decades.

Loading Instagram content

Seed dormancy is found in all flannel flower species.

"They all have this weird dormancy mechanism that responds to a variety of cues," Dr Offord says.

For flannel flowers that bloom after bushfire, the cues are typically smoke from fire awakening the seeds, and then rain.

But what "awakens" the sleeping flannel flower seeds can vary between locations and species.

"There's no one thing that will break that dormancy, no one thing that you can say, 'Oh, you do this,'" Dr Offord says.

"There's rain, smoke, wetting and drying cycles through the years, possibly heat. Also the length of time the seed has been in the soil.

"So there's no straightforward story around that, other than they do have this dormancy, which helps them to survive in sometimes hostile environments.'

Talara'tingi a significant D'harawal flower

For the D'harawal people, the flannel flower, known as Talara'tingi, is linked to one of their most significant places, says Gawaian Bodkin-Andrews, a D'harawal scholar at Western Sydney University.

"The story is that there was a time where children had not ever seen the Sun. A young girl, named Tiana travelled to a significant place and realised that the people had not been taking care of the country."

The story holds two important lessons: to remember the laws, protocols and need to look after country to ensure it is healthy, and to listen to the youth, who can also bring wisdom.

The dew from the flannel flower, collected before dawn, is a D'harawal treatment for severe grief. (ABC Mid North Coast: Meredith Kirton)

Hope and health was brought back to country and Tiana was gifted with the springing of the flannel flowers, shaped like a star and with leaves covered in a very fine type of fur that looks like frost.

Hence the name Talara'tingi, which means star of frost.

"The flowering of the flannel flower in the story indicated the ending of a long winter or maybe an ice age. Which gives an indication of how old this story truly is, and how long it's survived," Professor Bodkin-Andrews says.

You can grow them yourself (or buy a bunch)

Many years ago, Dr Offord worked with the cut flower industry to develop varieties of Actinotus helianthi suitable for cultivation.

"At one stage, they were only being harvested from the wild," she says.

"Now there are a few growers who cultivate flannel flowers and they have a much superior vase life and look beautiful."

Flannel flowers on NSW's north coast after bushfires. (ABC Mid North Coast: Emma Siossian)

While it's illegal to collect flannel flower plants or seeds without a permit, you can still grow them at home. Many nurseries sell the plants or seeds.

"They're quite self-sufficient," Dr Offord says.

"We generally suggest to grow them in pots. It's much easier to control their growth than in soil, because they do prefer to live in a somewhat light sandy soil.

"And they don't need a lot of fertiliser."

Where to see them in the wild

The flannel flower's sleeping seeds make it hard to predict where, or when, it might bloom.

"They can be quite ephemeral," Dr Offord says.

"You can have them growing somewhere and people will say, 'Oh, they're growing in a great abundance here.' You go back a few years later and they've gone."

The very tiny lesser flannel flower (Actinotus minor) is common around Sydney. (iNaturalist: Alistair Smith, CC BY-NC 4.0)

Yet, at some point, probably after a bushfire, the flowers will rise from the ashes like a floral phoenix, bringing hope and joy to those who see them whether in the wild or through media viewed across the world.

Definitely amazing!

World.title: At least 14 killed in 'despicable' Russian attack on shopping centre in Ukraine
World.content:
Ukrainian President Volodymr Zelenskyy has called a 'double-tap' Russian attack on a shopping centre that killed at least fourteen people in Kryvyi Rih "despicable".

About 120 others, including six children, were injured in the drone attack in the central Ukrainian city, according to local authorities.

"Twenty-one people are in serious condition, including one child," regional governor Oleksandr Hanzha said.

He posted a photo on the encrypted messaging app Telegram of black smoke billowing from a large industrial building.

AT least six people were killed and dozens injured in the attack on a shopping centre. ( State Emergency Service of Ukraine via Reuters)

Mr Zelenskyy has called the attack, which included one drone attack followed by a second as emergency services rushed to the scene, "absolutely cynical and despicable".

The Ukrainian president said a second Russian drone hit the shopping centre half an hour after the first in a deliberate attempt to target emergency services.

"Attacks like these are nothing less than terrorist acts," he said.

Kryvyi Rih has come under repeated Russian attacks throughout the war.

The industrial city lies roughly 60 kilometres from the front line.

The attack comes as Russia escalates its air war on Ukraine.

On Thursday, 17 people were killed in a Russian ballistic missile attack on the Ukrainian capital Kyiv.

The United Nations reported that the civilian death toll in 2026 had risen to its highest level since the first months of the war.

Ukraine has also stepped up its own attacks on Russia, targeting oil facilities and logistics infrastructure to try to undermine Moscow's ability to wage war.

Reuters

World.title: Man wielding sword injures several at high school in Sweden
World.content:
A man armed with a sword has injured several people at a high school in central Sweden.

At least two people have sustained serious injuries, according to emergency services.

After 2.20pm, local time, reports came through of an attack at Brinellskolan school in the municipality of Fagersta.

The local government said a person entered the school with a sword and injured several people.

Police said they had one person in custody and were investigating the incident.

"A call was received regarding a case of ongoing deadly violence at a school in Fagersta," police said in a statement.

The high school has about 450 students aged between 16 and 20.

Fagersta has a population of about 13,000 people and is located roughly 170km north west of Stockholm.

The local government authority has opened a crisis centre, offering support and information.

The school had just opened after a summer break and for some students it marked the first day at the senior high school.

Several other schools and public buildings in Fagersta were also placed in lockdown after the alleged sword attack. The lockdown was later lifted.

A student at the school, Abdulrahem Salmo, said he had seen a victim with a bloody stab wound in the arm.

"Then people called the police and we just all ran from there because we were afraid," he told SVT.

Local newspaper Fagersta-posten talked to Madelene Jansson outside the school, which her daughter had been attending.

"I first got a text message from her that somebody had been stabbed and that police were on the way. Then it all just went off. It feels unreal," she told the paper.

Swedish Prime Minister Ulf Kristersson said police were working intensively on the case and asked everyone to let them and the emergency services work undisturbed.

"Our thoughts are with all those affected," he posted on social media.

The incident comes more than a year after a school shooting in Orebro, when a gunman killed 10 people before turning the weapon on himself, in the worst mass shooting in Swedish history.

World.title: Prince Harry and others ordered to pay $17.8m legal costs to Daily Mail publisher
World.content:
Prince Harry, Elton John and a group of other high-profile claimants face the prospect of having to pay millions of pounds out of their own pockets to cover the legal costs of The Daily Mail's publisher, after a High Court judge ruled their failed privacy lawsuits were conducted in an unreasonable way.

The judge also ordered an interim payment of 9.54 million British pounds ($17.88 million) towards the legal costs of Associated Newspapers, which publishes The Daily Mail and other titles.

Last month, Justice Matthew Nicklin comprehensively rejected the case brought by Prince Harry, singer Elton John and five other figures, dismissing allegations that the Mail had engaged in widespread unlawful activities, such as phone hacking.

The Daily Mail's publisher argued Prince Harry and the other claimants had made wide-ranging, serious and "egregious" allegations against the paper without supporting evidence. (Reuters: Toby Melville)

Friday's judgment delivered another damaging blow to the claimants, ruling that the outstanding amount should be paid on an "indemnity basis".

This means that, as the losing party, the prince and the others must pay an amount towards Associated's legal costs without the publisher needing to show these were reasonable and proportionate.

Explaining his decision, Justice Nicklin was highly critical of the way the claimants' case had been put, including that serious allegations had rested on "speculative and inferential" foundations.

"In my judgment, the cumulative effect of these matters takes the case well outside the norm. The conduct was unreasonable to a high degree," the judge said.

A spokesperson for Prince Harry did not immediately respond to a request for comment from Reuters, while a spokesman for Associated Newspapers called the ruling "another overwhelming victory for the Mail and its journalism".

The court was told at a hearing in July that Associated had incurred a legal bill of 34.5 million British pounds ($65.6 million), while Prince Harry and other claimants only had an insurance policy which covered 16 million pounds ($30.4 million).

Associated's lawyer, Antony White, argued the claimants had made wide-ranging, serious and "egregious" allegations without supporting evidence, which had added to their costs.

He also said a statement made by the prince following the ruling was an abuse of his position and celebrity status.

Nicholas Bacon, the lawyer for the claimants, said in their submissions that Associated's 34.5 million-pound legal bill was "eye-watering", far exceeding an agreed budget.

Reuters

World.title: Federal government to fund majority of ACT gun buyback scheme
World.content:
The ACT will introduce a gun buyback scheme similar to the one in NSW, as part of a national push to strengthen Australia's gun laws.

What we do and don't know about guns in Australia Gun control researchers say we have "no idea" how many black market and 3D-printed weapons are out there.

The agreement between the federal and ACT governments comes after a National Cabinet commitment to "eradicate" antisemitism and strengthen gun laws following the Bondi Beach terrorist attack in December last year.

Last week, NSW announced it would be the first state to begin the national buyback scheme, commencing on November 2.

The ACT committed to being part of the scheme after it was announced in the wake of the attack, but until now has remained in negotiation with the federal government over how it would be funded.

The agreement will see the Commonwealth government fund 75 per cent of the buyback and associated administrative costs, and 100 per cent of the firearm destruction costs, with the ACT government funding the rest.

Prime Minister Anthony Albanese says national gun reform is important to ensure terrorist attacks like the one in Bondi cannot occur again. (ABC News: Matt Roberts)

Prime Minister Anthony Albanese said in a statement that the scheme was about taking action to keep communities safe.

"National gun reform is an important part of making sure an antisemitic terrorist attack like we saw at Bondi can't happen again," Mr Albanese said.

" I thank the ACT government for their collaboration as we work to take guns off our streets in order to better protect Australians. "

Currently there are about 23,000 firearms in the ACT, and over 7,000 people who hold a firearms licence.

About 14 per cent of those licence holders are expected to be affected by the proposed firearms cap.

No further details have been given about what date the scheme will begin in the territory, or what compensation will be offered per surrendered firearm.

'Some of the strongest firearms laws in the country'

ACT Chief Minister Andrew Barr acknowledged that the majority of firearms owners were responsible and law-abiding. (ABC News: Ian Cutmore)

In a statement, ACT Chief Minister Andrew Barr said the agreement with the federal government strengthened community safety, and supported effective firearm reforms across jurisdictions.

"Reducing the number of high-risk firearms in circulation is a sensible and practical measure to help keep Canberrans safer," he said.

"Working with the Commonwealth and NSW ensures a more coordinated approach to firearms safety.

" The ACT has some of the strongest firearms laws in the country and this agreement supports our ongoing efforts to further reduce the risk of firearms falling into the wrong hands. "

Mr Barr acknowledged that "the overwhelming majority" of licensed gun owners were responsible and law-abiding citizens.

Along with committing to the national buyback scheme, the ACT has also proposed a change to its gun laws. (ABC News: Keane Bourke)

"The buyback scheme will provide compensation while helping deliver further community safety outcomes," Mr Barr said.

The agreement also comes after the ACT government proposed new gun laws for the territory in February, which would see licensed gun holders limited to owning five guns.

The Firearms (Public Safety) Amendment Bill 2026 includes exemptions on that cap, allowing up to 10 guns for occupational and sporting purposes.

It would also criminalise the possession of blueprints for 3D-printed guns, prohibit belt-fed firearms, and re-categorise firearm types.

The bill is still before the ACT Legislative Assembly, and is expected to be debated during the assembly's spring sittings.

World.title: Labor and Coalition unite to ringfence AI from One Nation backlash
World.content:
Exclusive PoliticsFederalData centres Labor and Coalition unite to ringfence AI from One Nation backlash Paul Sakkal August 22, 2026 — 3:36am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Labor and the Coalition are nearing bipartisan consensus on AI, aiming to avoid a US-style backlash against data centres ahead of next week’s national cabinet meeting. In a new point of difference with One Nation, the Coalition has extended an olive branch to the prime minister on proposed AI regulations that will be discussed at Wednesday’s meeting of the national cabinet in Sydney. Opposition home affairs spokesman Jonno Duniam. Dominic Lorrimer Opposition home affairs spokesman Jonno Duniam said One Nation risked compromising Australia’s economic growth and national security if it ran a populist campaign against data centres, meaning it was “essential that the parties of government work together”. Duniam said the far-reaching innovation presented a once-in-a-generation chance to grow the economy and that a bipartisan consensus would help secure investment from international tech firms, hopefully allowing Australia to build its own AI products.



This masthead revealed earlier this month that Albanese was talking to the White House about securing first access to the most advanced models, known as frontier models. Australia could gain leverage with the US, currently locked in a battle for tech supremacy with China, by attracting firms such as Anthropic, which plans to invest $21 billion to make Australia a second home. Related Article Data centres How Albanese could force states to follow his lead on green energy data centres “One Nation needs to tell us if they’re not going to allow data centres to be built in Australia,” Duniam said in an interview with this masthead. “If they’re just a blanket ‘no’ on things like data centres, that puts us in that category of doing nothing, which means China wins. Chinese models will be here in Australia hoovering up our data and people will be using Chinese models, which we have no control over.” Senior figures in the government welcomed Duniam’s co-operative overtures, which could allow the major parties to forge an upbeat consensus on the AI debate that has eluded the US. The moves towards a bipartisan stance on AI caps a fortnight in which Labor and Coalition excluded One Nation and the Greens from deals on slashing the NDIS, forcing tech firms to fund journalism, and curbing gambling advertising. Opposition Leader Angus Taylor’s forces have been well behind Hanson in the polls. The deal-making has in part been driven by an intent to prove the Coalition’s ability to shape policy and sway outcomes.



Albanese gave a speech on AI last month aimed at convincing voters that AI firms would need to follow rules on energy and water use. Duniam said his olive branch was designed to tamp down populist campaigns and to make sure the sector “gets and keeps its social licence”. One Nation, surging in the polls, has talked up the AI opportunity, but Hanson has warned about self-regulation. In a social media post last week she put the US, Australia’s chief security ally, and China, on the same plane: “On AI, I believe we must protect Australian jobs and keep our data secure by building capacity here, not handing it to China or America.” The Greens have been campaigning for a moratorium on data centres. The Coalition is about to release a set of AI principles which are relatively similar to those released by Labor, focusing on productivity gains and making sure data centres did not suck up resources and were built in acceptable locations. One important sticking point is a feud over the use of fossil fuels to power data centres, which give firms such as Google, Anthropic and ChatGPT computing power to respond to searches, create new models, and produce videos. The energy market operator estimates that 6 per cent of the energy grid will be used to power data centres in 2030, up from 2 per cent now. Labor is already struggling to build enough wind and solar. Assistant Minister for Science, Technology and the Digital Economy Andrew Charlton. Rohan Thomson



Energy Minister Chris Bowen has taken a hard line, saying data centre operators must use green energy only. But others in the government have opened the door to the use of gas. The Albanese government has indicated it could steamroll conservative state governments of Queensland and NT at Wednesday’s national cabinet, where Albanese will seek in-principle support for his new national AI standards. Another national cabinet meeting will be held in October to formally sign off on the standards, which the government wants to put into law next year. Labor’s Assistant Minister for Science, Technology and the Digital Economy Andrew Charlton used a speech on Monday to say that Australia’s abundance of energy and land should be used to push Australia up the value chain. “Australia is playing in the bottom of the stack, in energy and data centres, but most of the real economic value is higher up in the chips, models, software and intellectual property,” he said.



Liberal MP Aaron Violi. The Sydney Morning Herald “The next step is using the data centre advantage and investment boom to grow our AI training ecosystem.” Coalition spokesman for science and technology Aaron Violi applauded a bipartisan committee on AI that was established by the parliament this week. “While AI has enormous potential to improve our lives and livelihoods, we cannot be and we are not complacent about the risks. This is why this committee will also examine the workforce and skills implications of AI job displacement but also job creation,” he said. Cut through the noise of federal politics with news, views and expert analysis. Subscribers can sign up to our weekly Inside Politics newsletter.

World.title: Revealed: The ‘lovesick’ letters Trump aide Natalie Harp sent her boss
World.content:
WorldNorth AmericaTrump's White House Revealed: The ‘lovesick’ letters Trump aide Natalie Harp sent her boss Michael Koziol August 22, 2026 — 2:39am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Washington: Personal letters from Natalie Harp to her boss Donald Trump have been revealed in full for the first time, shedding light on a relationship between the US president and one of his closest aides that has become the subject of intense scrutiny. Two letters, written by Harp during or immediately after a trip to the United Kingdom in 2023 – when Trump was out of office – reveal an aide deeply concerned about having upset or offended Trump in some way, and desperate to foster an intimate relationship with him. Natalie Harp, Donald Trump’s executive assistant, wrote letters to him that have been described as “lovesick” and “weird”. Getty Images The lengthy letters were published by author Michael Wolff and US news site The Daily Beast, to which Wolff is a regular contributor. Wolff said on a podcast he released the letters now because they showed a relationship “that should not exist in a professional setting”. In one, Harp asks for Trump’s forgiveness after apparently upsetting him during a golfing holiday to Scotland. “I was alone in the van outside Customs without my passport, I panicked, and I should have just called Secret Service instead of you,” she wrote.



“I also am sorry if I was an embarrassment walking the course in Scotland … If there is anything else I have done to cause you trouble, please forgive me. “I want things to always be right between us … I never want to bring you anything but joy. I’m sorry I lost my focus. You are all that matters to me. I don’t want to ever let you down. Thank you for being my Guardian and Protector in this Life.” Trump and Harp appear together at a 2023 golf tournament at Trump’s Bedminster Golf Club, where Harp allegedly spent a summer sleeping in a locker room. NYT That letter was signed: “With all my heart, Natalie.” In a subsequent letter to Trump, Harp said the UK trip gave her a chance to learn about herself and unplug. “I didn’t have to be ‘Human Printer’,” she said, a reference to her job of printing off news and complimentary articles for Trump to read.



“With so much thinking time, I confess it did have a slightly negative effect at times, that I know you picked up on, but the end result, I believe, will be worth it. “I had no idea how rapidly I was approaching burnout, and starting to envoy those whose only ‘job’ seems to be to talk with you, and look pretty. I want that job!!! Natalie Harp this week disembarking Marine One with President Donald Trump following a weekend in New Jersey at his golf club. Getty Images “So many times, I’m just trying to stay afloat with all that’s coming in for you, I look like a hunchback who didn’t have time to freshen up (at least you know what I should look like)! “I miss the days when you used to call, during my Talkshow days, and we’d talk about everything and nothing. I want to get back to that synergy. We shouldn’t have to talk about work all the time!!”



Harp went on to tell Trump she needed to reunite her “past self” with her current person to become the best version of herself and “make you proud”. Related Article Trump's White House Innuendo and rumour: Who is Natalie Harp, the ‘human printer’ who follows Trump everywhere? “Please, when I fail, will you tell me?” she wrote. “You have the absolute right to cuss me out, if need be, when I deserve it, because no one knows or cares about me more. “To modify a classic, ‘I could not have parted with you, to anyone less worthy’ - And, I will add, it is I who is unworthy.” That letter was signed: “Always, Natalie.” Excerpts of the letters had previously been published by The New York Times. Wolff described the content as “lovesick”, “submissive” and “weird”, and said while he did not believe Harp was Trump’s girlfriend, they were evidence of an inappropriate relationship between the president and a workplace subordinate.



“The relationship here is not a relationship that should exist in a professional setting,” he said on The Daily Beast’s Inside Trump’s Head podcast. “This ain’t normal.” Harp, 35, joined Trump’s staff while he was out of office and worked on his 2024 election campaign. Since his return to the Oval Office, she has served as executive assistant to the president, including drafting and posting his remarks on Truth Social – his preferred method of communication. Natalie Harp in the Oval Office during a meeting to sign an executive order about vaccines. AP Photo/Jacquelyn Martin Contacted for comment, White House spokesman Davis Ingle told this masthead Harp was one of the most loyal and hardest-working aides on the president’s team. “The Fake News’s continued attacks on President Trump and his Administration prove exactly why trust in media is at historic lows,” he said. “The media should focus on reporting real news and stop trying to smear dedicated public servants.”



Harp was thrust into the spotlight last weekend after Democratic senator and potential presidential candidate Jon Ossoff told a rally that Trump would rather travel on his plane “with Natalie” than do his job. Related Article US politics ‘Be quiet’: Trump berates reporter who asked about his relationship with female staffer That was a reference to Harp being one of a handful of aides selected by Trump to take a secret flight out of last month’s NATO summit in Turkey, rather than travel on “Air Force One”, which had been deemed a security risk amid threats from Iran. Multiple senior aides and cabinet secretaries were left to travel on the Boeing 747 – as well as the travelling press pack, who were not told of the security risk or that Trump was not on board. On Wednesday, MS-NOW revealed Harp had worked in the White House and Trump’s inner circle for more than a year without receiving a security clearance. MS-NOW reported that Trump intervened amid rising concerns from security officials and White House lawyers, and that she now has a clearance.



David Axelrod, a Democratic strategist who was chief-of-staff to Barack Obama as president, said if it was true that “the person closest to [Trump] and his thinking on a daily basis has no security clearance and refuses to submit to the process of getting it, it’s a deadly serious issue”. Axelrod was previously critical of Ossoff’s decision to raise Harp at his rally, saying it “seemed gratuitous and unnecessary”. Trump’s allies accused Ossoff of trafficking in innuendo and smearing a public servant with the implication she was having a sexual relationship with her boss. Trump, when asked during the week for a response to Ossoff’s remarks, said that Ossoff looked like Pee-wee Herman, the childish comedy character created by Paul Reubens.
