World.title: Prince Harry, celebrities ordered to pay $18m – but final court bill could be higher
World.content:
WorldEuropeRoyal family Prince Harry, celebrities ordered to pay $18m – but final court bill could be higher David Crowe August 22, 2026 — 1:41am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Prince Harry has been ordered to pay a steep legal bill for his failed court case against a major publisher after a court ruled that he and his fellow claimants owed £9.54 million ($18.1 million) in legal costs. The court ruling exposes Harry and others, including rock star Elton John and model Elizabeth Hurley, to even greater costs after a judge dismissed their long-running claim against the Daily Mail earlier this year. Prince Harry, the Duke of Sussex, at a roundtable for support for veterans in Washington on Wednesday. AP Photo/Alex Brandon They must pay the first sum by August 28 and face a difficult legal argument over the remainder of the costs, given the Mail’s publisher won the case and wants the prince and others to cover its costs. Lawyers for the publisher, Associated Newspapers, told the court in July that its legal bill had reached £34.5 million ($65.6 million).



Related Article Royal family ‘Obvious whitewash’: Prince Harry lashes judge after losing Daily Mail privacy case Harry and other claimants arranged an insurance policy to cover £16 ⁠million ($30 million), but are now exposed to a much steeper bill that could require them to pay from their own savings. Judge Matthew Nicklin’s judgment on costs was published on Friday in London (early on Saturday AEST). Nicklin was highly critical of the way the claimants’ case had been put, saying their allegations were based on “speculative and inferential” foundations and had not been withdrawn when they were no longer being pursued. “In my judgment, the cumulative effect of these matters takes the case well outside the norm. The conduct was unreasonable to a high degree,” Nicklin said.



The High Court ruled in July that the Duke of Sussex and the other claimants had failed to prove their allegations that the Daily Mail had used unlawful means, including phone hacking, to get stories about them. They also claimed it used “blagging” – a practice in which a journalist makes false claims to trick people into divulging information. Associated Newspapers said at the time that the ruling was “an overwhelming victory for the Daily Mail and its journalists and for a free press generally”. The claimants who joined Harry in the case were Hurley, actor Sadie Frost, politician Simon Hughes and Baroness Doreen Lawrence, a member of the House of Lords whose son was murdered in a racist attack. John joined the case with his husband, David Furnish. Actor and model Elizabeth Hurley arrives at court with her son, Damian, in January. AFP





“It is a complete and obvious whitewash, but sadly not altogether unexpected. However, the lengths to which the court has gone to exonerate the Mail is as shocking as it is totally unwarranted,” they said. Related Article Royal family Harry and Meghan are returning to the UK. Who will keep them safe? “When the court says there is not sufficient evidence of wrongdoing, despite the documents showing otherwise, then one does wonder how justice was ever going to be achieved.” Lawyers for the newspaper called that statement as an abuse of the prince’s celebrity status. The newspaper is controlled by Jonathan Vere Harmsworth, the hereditary peer Viscount Rothermere, whose great-grandfather founded the Daily Mail in 1896.



In a statement on Friday, the publisher hailed the initial decision on costs as another “overwhelming victory” for the Mail and its journalism. If the two sides cannot agree on the rest of the costs, they will head to separate litigation to decide the bill. Nicholas Bacon, KC, the lawyer for the claimants, said in their submissions that Associated’s £34.5 million ($65.6 million) legal bill was “eye-watering” and ⁠far exceeding an agreed budget. With Reuters Get a note directly from our foreign correspondents on what’s making headlines around the world.

World.title: The moment that might have ended the most storied of Collingwood careers
World.content:
SportAFLAFL 2026 The moment that might have ended the most storied of Collingwood careers Michael Gleeson August 22, 2026 — 1:16am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Loading

Scott Pendlebury jogged slowly to the bench favouring his leg. It might be the last time he is seen in a Collingwood jumper on the MCG. It was an utterly nondescript moment in the most storied of careers. Pendlebury felt a strain at the back of his knee that might have been a bursar, might have been a hamstring strain, and might just be the injury that puts a stop on his finals series. Scott Pendlebury walks from the ground with his Collingwood playing future in doubt. Getty Images Last year’s preliminary final has to be in Craig McRae’s mind as he ponders the fitness of probably the club’s greatest-ever player. Last year, also against the Brisbane Lions, he tore a calf in the warm-up. A soft tissue injury again for a now 38-year-old, on the eve of the finals, will weigh on McRae. And Pendlebury. If it is to be his last game for Collingwood, it could not have been a more anticlimactic departure. No garlands, no lines of honour, no chairing off, no kids through the banner, just a night sitting on the bench in his slides, eating chicken wraps and watching his team get belted.



It was the sort of moment that might encourage the idea that we don’t want him to go out this way – and he doesn’t either – so he plays on. As McRae said, those are conversations for another day. But that moment punctuated what was a very strange game. View post on X The AFL expanded the finals to 10 teams and introduced the wildcard round to engender interest in the last rounds of the home-and-away season. Ironically, this game would have had more interest were it held under last year’s rules. Collingwood could not drop below 10th, and so were battling to finish either eighth or ninth. In other words, last year they would have had to win to play finals. Instead, this game was played with the passion of a polka.



Collingwood’s game is predicated on furious intensity and defensive fight. None were present in a game where 40 goals were kicked and no one wanted to defend. It was a case for the prosecution who say high scoring and exciting football are two different things. View post on X That is not to diminish the Lions’ effort for they outplayed Collingwood. They beat them by 54 points earlier this year and they are plainly a better team. But we knew that. One team has won the past two flags and sits now in third place, and Collingwood needed a wildcard round to be sure of playing finals. “It was really hard as a coach because you’re seeing us not do things we’ve been doing,” McRae said. “I go, ‘Oh, what are we doing? Like, this is a trademark’ … I think there was a period of the game where it looked like both teams wanted to get to next week quickly. It can happen this time of year for teams that aren’t playing for much.”



Logan Morris is still only scratching the surface of what he could become. AFL Photos As it was, the interest was in Logan Morris. It is exciting – or frightening, depending on your perspective – to think that Morris has two flags already and is yet to even get close to being the dominant player he is becoming. There was a world in which Morris might have been at Collingwood. If the idea of what the club missed out on has haunted them since, the reality of what he has become was a living nightmare on the MCG. Morris kicked eight and could have had 10. In his draft year – and yes, every other club with a selection would have taken him before pick No.31 had they known what he would become – Collingwood agonised over the decision but were troubled that he was an in-between size and would not be a key forward. They chose Harry De Mattia instead at No.25. He is yet to play a senior game. Morris was outstanding, and with Oscar Allen and Eric Hipwood they had their way with Collingwood’s depleted backline missing Darcy Moore, Isaac Quaynor and Harry Perryman and with Jeremy Howe on managed minutes.



Liam Puncher was playing SANFL footy only a couple of months ago. He might have preferred West Torrens after the night he had on the MCG with the ball coming in the way it was. Lachie Neale played the sort of game that would have had the boxes of both coaches asking questions. Chris Fagan will have looked at his 16 clearances, yes 16, and wondered, ‘How can we let him and Zac Bailey potentially leave?’ Craig Mcrae and Collingwood will have said, ‘If we had misgivings about a 32-year-old free agent before, we don’t now’. For the Lions, this game was about jockeying to try and make sure they played the team everyone now wants to play in the finals, Sydney. They should have safeguarded that. The draw with Collingwood last week is all the more galling for the Hawks this week, given the Swans are now a shattered club and a team you’d far rather play than any other in these finals (this is obviously an observation through a football lens on the season, and plainly not a comment on what occurred in the Pullman hotel to precipitate this change at Sydney).



Editor's pick AFL 2026 ‘We were keen on him, the coaches weren’t’: How this star slipped to the Lions The Hawks now need to win by nigh on 100 points over West Coast to boost their percentage enough to jump the Lions and play Sydney in the first final, not Fremantle in WA. Its doable, but the way they played last week you would not think likely unless the Eagles play like they want their holidays to start. That is the hard bit for interpreting this game. The Lions showed they are exceptional and have as complete a forward set-up, with the best young key forward in the game, as they do defensive set-up. They don’t lack for anything across the ground, other than perhaps some smarts from Ty Gallop, a player just back from an idiotic three-game suspension for slamming Mitch Georgiades’ head into the turf, only to tackle Charlie West into the ground with both arms pinned. But then Dayne Zorko elbowing Jack Crisp in the face with a late smother of a handball is also a contender for unnecessarily risky actions. Keep up to date with the best AFL coverage in the country.

World.title: World No.1 Jannik Sinner withdraws from US Open due to injury
World.content:
SportTennisUS Open World No.1 Jannik Sinner withdraws from US Open due to injury Karan Prashant Saxena and Pearl Josephine Nazare August 22, 2026 — 12:30am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

World No.1 Jannik Sinner has withdrawn from the US Open due to a persistent right knee injury, the Italian said on Friday, depriving the season’s final grand slam of one of its biggest contenders. The 24-year-old, who captured his fifth major title at Wimbledon last month, has not played since sustaining the injury earlier this month. Jannik Sinner successfully defended his Wimbledon title in July. Getty He pulled out of the Cincinnati Open and also skipped the Canadian Open, two key hard-court tune-up events ahead of the grand slam tournament in New York. “Even though I have been working hard with my team and my medical staff, we have now had to make the difficult decision that I will not be able to compete at the US Open this year,” Sinner said in a statement on X.



View post on X “We have been back on court in Monte Carlo over the last couple of days and have realised that I still need more time to recover from my right knee issue. “I’m obviously very sad and disappointed, as New York has a special place in my heart.” The announcement comes a day after world No.2 Carlos Alcaraz confirmed he would compete at Flushing Meadows following a four-month absence from competitive tennis. View post on X



Alcaraz, who beat Sinner in last year’s US Open final, now heads to New York as the highest-ranked player and one of the favourites to lift the title, despite recent injury troubles. Related Article Wimbledon Sinner wins back-to-back Wimbledon titles, shows ‘why he’s the best player in the world’ The US Open runs from August 23 to September 13. Sinner’s absence removes one of the Spaniard’s biggest rivals and could ease his path as he bids for an eighth grand slam crown. Britain’s Jack Draper has also withdrawn from the US Open, with the Lawn Tennis Association announcing his absence hours after Sinner pulled out of the event.



While the LTA did not disclose the nature of Draper’s injury, media reports said the 24-year-old withdrew because of a long-term left arm problem. Draper climbed to a career-high ranking of world No.4 in 2025 but was forced to cut short his season because of a bone injury in his arm. He has also battled a knee injury this year. Britain’s Jack Draper, pictured during the Cincinnati Open, has withdrawn from the US Open. Getty Images Now ranked 143rd, Draper suffered early exits in Montreal and Cincinnati. His best Grand Slam performance came at the 2024 US Open, where he reached the semi-finals.

World.title: The Herald picks up five awards as excellence in journalism celebrated
World.content:
PoliticsNSWMedia & marketing The Herald picks up five awards as excellence in journalism celebrated August 21, 2026 — 10:30pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

An investigation that revealed the NRL’s top referee had a gambling problem, photographs capturing the Bondi Beach terror attack, and a profile of Australia’s cardboard king are part of the Herald’s award-winning coverage celebrated at the Kennedy Foundation’s Excellence in Journalism awards. The awards, across 37 total categories, were announced at a ceremony at Sydney’s Royal Randwick Racecourse on Friday night. Edwina Pickles has been recognised for her photographic coverage of the Bondi Beach terror attack. Edwina Pickles Senior sports reporter Chris Barrett won the Outstanding Sport Reporting category for an investigation revealing rugby league’s most high-profile referee, Ashley Klein, had a $400,000 gambling problem, which the code knew about for four years while letting him continue to officiate matches at the top level. Photographer Edwina Pickles won the Outstanding News Photography category for her coverage of the Bondi Beach terror attack in December.



Deputy state topic editor Michael Ruffles won the Outstanding Three Headlines category. Among his submissions was “The lying, the Ferrari wish and $400,000 in cash in the wardrobe”, which related to chief investigative reporter Kate McClymont’s coverage of former bankrupt Warren Jack’s “fanciful” explanations to a Sydney court during a dispute over unpaid loans. Cartoonist Matt Golding picked up the Outstanding Cartoon award for “Playing Trump”, which depicted Russian President Vladimir Putin passing the dice to Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu as the pair play a board game called “Trump” with North Korea’s Supreme Leader Kim Jong-un and Chinese President Xi Jinping. Cartoonist Matt Golding has been won for his “Playing Trump” cartoon. Matt Golding Jane Cadzow won Outstanding Feature Writing for “In The Box Seat”, her Good Weekend profile of cardboard king Anthony Pratt, the boss of Visy packaging and one of Australia’s richest men, published in the Herald and The Age. The Age’s veteran crime reporter, John Silvester, also won Outstanding Columnist for his regular Naked City column lifting the lid on Australia’s criminal underworld.



The Herald was nominated for a total of 20 awards, the most of any news organisation in Australia, winning five categories. Related Article Media & marketing Herald scoops young journalist prizes Herald editor Jordan Baker said she was enormously proud of the publication’s winners and finalists. “The recognition of the Herald across so many areas – sport reporting, feature writing, headlines, photography and cartoons – illustrates the depth of talent in our newsroom. “It is also a reflection of the Herald’s commitment to serving our subscribers and telling Sydney’s stories,” Baker said.



The foundation said the 2026 awards attracted a record number of entries. “It’s been another bumper year for excellent Australian journalism, and there’s no greater honour than to receive a Kennedy for your work,” Kennedy Foundation chair Carl Dumbrell said. “The Kennedy Foundation is extremely proud of its support for those endeavours that are essential to an informed and vital democracy.” Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights.

World.title: Labor and Coalition unite to ringfence AI from One Nation backlash
World.content:
Exclusive PoliticsFederalData centres Labor and Coalition unite to ringfence AI from One Nation backlash Paul Sakkal August 22, 2026 — 3:36am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Labor and the Coalition are nearing bipartisan consensus on AI, aiming to avoid a US-style backlash against data centres ahead of next week’s national cabinet meeting. In a new point of difference with One Nation, the Coalition has extended an olive branch to the prime minister on proposed AI regulations that will be discussed at Wednesday’s meeting of the national cabinet in Sydney. Opposition home affairs spokesman Jonno Duniam. Dominic Lorrimer Opposition home affairs spokesman Jonno Duniam said One Nation risked compromising Australia’s economic growth and national security if it ran a populist campaign against data centres, meaning it was “essential that the parties of government work together”. Duniam said the far-reaching innovation presented a once-in-a-generation chance to grow the economy and that a bipartisan consensus would help secure investment from international tech firms, hopefully allowing Australia to build its own AI products.



This masthead revealed earlier this month that Albanese was talking to the White House about securing first access to the most advanced models, known as frontier models. Australia could gain leverage with the US, currently locked in a battle for tech supremacy with China, by attracting firms such as Anthropic, which plans to invest $21 billion to make Australia a second home. Related Article Data centres How Albanese could force states to follow his lead on green energy data centres “One Nation needs to tell us if they’re not going to allow data centres to be built in Australia,” Duniam said in an interview with this masthead. “If they’re just a blanket ‘no’ on things like data centres, that puts us in that category of doing nothing, which means China wins. Chinese models will be here in Australia hoovering up our data and people will be using Chinese models, which we have no control over.” Senior figures in the government welcomed Duniam’s co-operative overtures, which could allow the major parties to forge an upbeat consensus on the AI debate that has eluded the US. The moves towards a bipartisan stance on AI caps a fortnight in which Labor and Coalition excluded One Nation and the Greens from deals on slashing the NDIS, forcing tech firms to fund journalism, and curbing gambling advertising. Opposition Leader Angus Taylor’s forces have been well behind Hanson in the polls. The deal-making has in part been driven by an intent to prove the Coalition’s ability to shape policy and sway outcomes.



Albanese gave a speech on AI last month aimed at convincing voters that AI firms would need to follow rules on energy and water use. Duniam said his olive branch was designed to tamp down populist campaigns and to make sure the sector “gets and keeps its social licence”. One Nation, surging in the polls, has talked up the AI opportunity, but Hanson has warned about self-regulation. In a social media post last week she put the US, Australia’s chief security ally, and China, on the same plane: “On AI, I believe we must protect Australian jobs and keep our data secure by building capacity here, not handing it to China or America.” The Greens have been campaigning for a moratorium on data centres. The Coalition is about to release a set of AI principles which are relatively similar to those released by Labor, focusing on productivity gains and making sure data centres did not suck up resources and were built in acceptable locations. One important sticking point is a feud over the use of fossil fuels to power data centres, which give firms such as Google, Anthropic and ChatGPT computing power to respond to searches, create new models, and produce videos. The energy market operator estimates that 6 per cent of the energy grid will be used to power data centres in 2030, up from 2 per cent now. Labor is already struggling to build enough wind and solar. Assistant Minister for Science, Technology and the Digital Economy Andrew Charlton. Rohan Thomson



Energy Minister Chris Bowen has taken a hard line, saying data centre operators must use green energy only. But others in the government have opened the door to the use of gas. The Albanese government has indicated it could steamroll conservative state governments of Queensland and NT at Wednesday’s national cabinet, where Albanese will seek in-principle support for his new national AI standards. Another national cabinet meeting will be held in October to formally sign off on the standards, which the government wants to put into law next year. Labor’s Assistant Minister for Science, Technology and the Digital Economy Andrew Charlton used a speech on Monday to say that Australia’s abundance of energy and land should be used to push Australia up the value chain. “Australia is playing in the bottom of the stack, in energy and data centres, but most of the real economic value is higher up in the chips, models, software and intellectual property,” he said.



Liberal MP Aaron Violi. The Sydney Morning Herald “The next step is using the data centre advantage and investment boom to grow our AI training ecosystem.” Coalition spokesman for science and technology Aaron Violi applauded a bipartisan committee on AI that was established by the parliament this week. “While AI has enormous potential to improve our lives and livelihoods, we cannot be and we are not complacent about the risks. This is why this committee will also examine the workforce and skills implications of AI job displacement but also job creation,” he said. World.title: Revealed: The ‘lovesick’ letters Trump aide Natalie Harp sent her boss
World.content:
WorldNorth AmericaTrump's White House Revealed: The ‘lovesick’ letters Trump aide Natalie Harp sent her boss Michael Koziol August 22, 2026 — 2:39am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Washington: Personal letters from Natalie Harp to her boss Donald Trump have been revealed in full for the first time, shedding light on a relationship between the US president and one of his closest aides that has become the subject of intense scrutiny. Two letters, written by Harp during or immediately after a trip to the United Kingdom in 2023 – when Trump was out of office – reveal an aide deeply concerned about having upset or offended Trump in some way, and desperate to foster an intimate relationship with him. Natalie Harp, Donald Trump’s executive assistant, wrote letters to him that have been described as “lovesick” and “weird”. Getty Images The lengthy letters were published by author Michael Wolff and US news site The Daily Beast, to which Wolff is a regular contributor. Wolff said on a podcast he released the letters now because they showed a relationship “that should not exist in a professional setting”. In one, Harp asks for Trump’s forgiveness after apparently upsetting him during a golfing holiday to Scotland. “I was alone in the van outside Customs without my passport, I panicked, and I should have just called Secret Service instead of you,” she wrote.



“I also am sorry if I was an embarrassment walking the course in Scotland … If there is anything else I have done to cause you trouble, please forgive me. “I want things to always be right between us … I never want to bring you anything but joy. I’m sorry I lost my focus. You are all that matters to me. I don’t want to ever let you down. Thank you for being my Guardian and Protector in this Life.” Trump and Harp appear together at a 2023 golf tournament at Trump’s Bedminster Golf Club, where Harp allegedly spent a summer sleeping in a locker room. NYT That letter was signed: “With all my heart, Natalie.” In a subsequent letter to Trump, Harp said the UK trip gave her a chance to learn about herself and unplug. “I didn’t have to be ‘Human Printer’,” she said, a reference to her job of printing off news and complimentary articles for Trump to read.



“With so much thinking time, I confess it did have a slightly negative effect at times, that I know you picked up on, but the end result, I believe, will be worth it. “I had no idea how rapidly I was approaching burnout, and starting to envoy those whose only ‘job’ seems to be to talk with you, and look pretty. I want that job!!! Natalie Harp this week disembarking Marine One with President Donald Trump following a weekend in New Jersey at his golf club. Getty Images “So many times, I’m just trying to stay afloat with all that’s coming in for you, I look like a hunchback who didn’t have time to freshen up (at least you know what I should look like)! “I miss the days when you used to call, during my Talkshow days, and we’d talk about everything and nothing. I want to get back to that synergy. We shouldn’t have to talk about work all the time!!”



Harp went on to tell Trump she needed to reunite her “past self” with her current person to become the best version of herself and “make you proud”. Related Article Trump's White House Innuendo and rumour: Who is Natalie Harp, the ‘human printer’ who follows Trump everywhere? “Please, when I fail, will you tell me?” she wrote. “You have the absolute right to cuss me out, if need be, when I deserve it, because no one knows or cares about me more. “To modify a classic, ‘I could not have parted with you, to anyone less worthy’ - And, I will add, it is I who is unworthy.” That letter was signed: “Always, Natalie.” Excerpts of the letters had previously been published by The New York Times. Wolff described the content as “lovesick”, “submissive” and “weird”, and said while he did not believe Harp was Trump’s girlfriend, they were evidence of an inappropriate relationship between the president and a workplace subordinate.



“The relationship here is not a relationship that should exist in a professional setting,” he said on The Daily Beast’s Inside Trump’s Head podcast. “This ain’t normal.” Harp, 35, joined Trump’s staff while he was out of office and worked on his 2024 election campaign. Since his return to the Oval Office, she has served as executive assistant to the president, including drafting and posting his remarks on Truth Social – his preferred method of communication. Natalie Harp in the Oval Office during a meeting to sign an executive order about vaccines. AP Photo/Jacquelyn Martin Contacted for comment, White House spokesman Davis Ingle told this masthead Harp was one of the most loyal and hardest-working aides on the president’s team. “The Fake News’s continued attacks on President Trump and his Administration prove exactly why trust in media is at historic lows,” he said. “The media should focus on reporting real news and stop trying to smear dedicated public servants.”



Harp was thrust into the spotlight last weekend after Democratic senator and potential presidential candidate Jon Ossoff told a rally that Trump would rather travel on his plane “with Natalie” than do his job. Related Article US politics ‘Be quiet’: Trump berates reporter who asked about his relationship with female staffer That was a reference to Harp being one of a handful of aides selected by Trump to take a secret flight out of last month’s NATO summit in Turkey, rather than travel on “Air Force One”, which had been deemed a security risk amid threats from Iran. Multiple senior aides and cabinet secretaries were left to travel on the Boeing 747 – as well as the travelling press pack, who were not told of the security risk or that Trump was not on board. On Wednesday, MS-NOW revealed Harp had worked in the White House and Trump’s inner circle for more than a year without receiving a security clearance. MS-NOW reported that Trump intervened amid rising concerns from security officials and White House lawyers, and that she now has a clearance.



David Axelrod, a Democratic strategist who was chief-of-staff to Barack Obama as president, said if it was true that “the person closest to [Trump] and his thinking on a daily basis has no security clearance and refuses to submit to the process of getting it, it’s a deadly serious issue”. Axelrod was previously critical of Ossoff’s decision to raise Harp at his rally, saying it “seemed gratuitous and unnecessary”. Trump’s allies accused Ossoff of trafficking in innuendo and smearing a public servant with the implication she was having a sexual relationship with her boss. Trump, when asked during the week for a response to Ossoff’s remarks, said that Ossoff looked like Pee-wee Herman, the childish comedy character created by Paul Reubens. World.title: Prince Harry, celebrities ordered to pay $18m – but final court bill could be higher
World.content:
WorldEuropeRoyal family Prince Harry, celebrities ordered to pay $18m – but final court bill could be higher David Crowe August 22, 2026 — 1:41am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Prince Harry has been ordered to pay a steep legal bill for his failed court case against a major publisher after a court ruled that he and his fellow claimants owed £9.54 million ($18.1 million) in legal costs. The court ruling exposes Harry and others, including rock star Elton John and model Elizabeth Hurley, to even greater costs after a judge dismissed their long-running claim against the Daily Mail earlier this year. Prince Harry, the Duke of Sussex, at a roundtable for support for veterans in Washington on Wednesday. AP Photo/Alex Brandon They must pay the first sum by August 28 and face a difficult legal argument over the remainder of the costs, given the Mail’s publisher won the case and wants the prince and others to cover its costs. Lawyers for the publisher, Associated Newspapers, told the court in July that its legal bill had reached £34.5 million ($65.6 million).



Related Article Royal family ‘Obvious whitewash’: Prince Harry lashes judge after losing Daily Mail privacy case Harry and other claimants arranged an insurance policy to cover £16 ⁠million ($30 million), but are now exposed to a much steeper bill that could require them to pay from their own savings. Judge Matthew Nicklin’s judgment on costs was published on Friday in London (early on Saturday AEST). Nicklin was highly critical of the way the claimants’ case had been put, saying their allegations were based on “speculative and inferential” foundations and had not been withdrawn when they were no longer being pursued. “In my judgment, the cumulative effect of these matters takes the case well outside the norm. The conduct was unreasonable to a high degree,” Nicklin said.



The High Court ruled in July that the Duke of Sussex and the other claimants had failed to prove their allegations that the Daily Mail had used unlawful means, including phone hacking, to get stories about them. They also claimed it used “blagging” – a practice in which a journalist makes false claims to trick people into divulging information. Associated Newspapers said at the time that the ruling was “an overwhelming victory for the Daily Mail and its journalists and for a free press generally”. The claimants who joined Harry in the case were Hurley, actor Sadie Frost, politician Simon Hughes and Baroness Doreen Lawrence, a member of the House of Lords whose son was murdered in a racist attack. John joined the case with his husband, David Furnish. Actor and model Elizabeth Hurley arrives at court with her son, Damian, in January. AFP





“It is a complete and obvious whitewash, but sadly not altogether unexpected. However, the lengths to which the court has gone to exonerate the Mail is as shocking as it is totally unwarranted,” they said. Related Article Royal family Harry and Meghan are returning to the UK. Who will keep them safe? “When the court says there is not sufficient evidence of wrongdoing, despite the documents showing otherwise, then one does wonder how justice was ever going to be achieved.” Lawyers for the newspaper called that statement as an abuse of the prince’s celebrity status. The newspaper is controlled by Jonathan Vere Harmsworth, the hereditary peer Viscount Rothermere, whose great-grandfather founded the Daily Mail in 1896.



In a statement on Friday, the publisher hailed the initial decision on costs as another “overwhelming victory” for the Mail and its journalism. If the two sides cannot agree on the rest of the costs, they will head to separate litigation to decide the bill. Nicholas Bacon, KC, the lawyer for the claimants, said in their submissions that Associated’s £34.5 million ($65.6 million) legal bill was “eye-watering” and ⁠far exceeding an agreed budget. Scott Pendlebury walks from the ground with his Collingwood playing future in doubt. No garlands, no lines of honour, no chairing off, no kids through the banner, just a night sitting on the bench in his slides, eating chicken wraps and watching his team get belted.

World.title: World No.1 Jannik Sinner withdraws from US Open due to injury
World.content:
SportTennisUS Open World No.1 Jannik Sinner withdraws from US Open due to injury Karan Prashant Saxena and Pearl Josephine Nazare August 22, 2026 — 12:30am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

World No.1 Jannik Sinner has withdrawn from the US Open due to a persistent right knee injury, the Italian said on Friday, depriving the season’s final grand slam of one of its biggest contenders. The 24-year-old, who captured his fifth major title at Wimbledon last month, has not played since sustaining the injury earlier this month. Jannik Sinner successfully defended his Wimbledon title in July. Getty He pulled out of the Cincinnati Open and also skipped the Canadian Open, two key hard-court tune-up events ahead of the grand slam tournament in New York. “Even though I have been working hard with my team and my medical staff, we have now had to make the difficult decision that I will not be able to compete at the US Open this year,” Sinner said in a statement on X.



View post on X “We have been back on court in Monte Carlo over the last couple of days and have realised that I still need more time to recover from my right knee issue. “I’m obviously very sad and disappointed, as New York has a special place in my heart.” The announcement comes a day after world No.2 Carlos Alcaraz confirmed he would compete at Flushing Meadows following a four-month absence from competitive tennis. View post on X



Alcaraz, who beat Sinner in last year’s US Open final, now heads to New York as the highest-ranked player and one of the favourites to lift the title, despite recent injury troubles. Related Article Wimbledon Sinner wins back-to-back Wimbledon titles, shows ‘why he’s the best player in the world’ The US Open runs from August 23 to September 13. Sinner’s absence removes one of the Spaniard’s biggest rivals and could ease his path as he bids for an eighth grand slam crown. Britain’s Jack Draper has also withdrawn from the US Open, with the Lawn Tennis Association announcing his absence hours after Sinner pulled out of the event.



While the LTA did not disclose the nature of Draper’s injury, media reports said the 24-year-old withdrew because of a long-term left arm problem. Draper climbed to a career-high ranking of world No.4 in 2025 but was forced to cut short his season because of a bone injury in his arm. He has also battled a knee injury this year. Britain’s Jack Draper, pictured during the Cincinnati Open, has withdrawn from the US Open. Getty Images Now ranked 143rd, Draper suffered early exits in Montreal and Cincinnati. His best Grand Slam performance came at the 2024 US Open, where he reached the semi-finals.

World.title: The Herald picks up five awards as excellence in journalism celebrated
World.content:
PoliticsNSWMedia & marketing The Herald picks up five awards as excellence in journalism celebrated August 21, 2026 — 10:30pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

An investigation that revealed the NRL’s top referee had a gambling problem, photographs capturing the Bondi Beach terror attack, and a profile of Australia’s cardboard king are part of the Herald’s award-winning coverage celebrated at the Kennedy Foundation’s Excellence in Journalism awards. The awards, across 37 total categories, were announced at a ceremony at Sydney’s Royal Randwick Racecourse on Friday night. Edwina Pickles has been recognised for her photographic coverage of the Bondi Beach terror attack. Edwina Pickles Senior sports reporter Chris Barrett won the Outstanding Sport Reporting category for an investigation revealing rugby league’s most high-profile referee, Ashley Klein, had a $400,000 gambling problem, which the code knew about for four years while letting him continue to officiate matches at the top level. Photographer Edwina Pickles won the Outstanding News Photography category for her coverage of the Bondi Beach terror attack in December.



Deputy state topic editor Michael Ruffles won the Outstanding Three Headlines category. Among his submissions was “The lying, the Ferrari wish and $400,000 in cash in the wardrobe”, which related to chief investigative reporter Kate McClymont’s coverage of former bankrupt Warren Jack’s “fanciful” explanations to a Sydney court during a dispute over unpaid loans. Cartoonist Matt Golding picked up the Outstanding Cartoon award for “Playing Trump”, which depicted Russian President Vladimir Putin passing the dice to Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu as the pair play a board game called “Trump” with North Korea’s Supreme Leader Kim Jong-un and Chinese President Xi Jinping. Cartoonist Matt Golding has been won for his “Playing Trump” cartoon. Matt Golding Jane Cadzow won Outstanding Feature Writing for “In The Box Seat”, her Good Weekend profile of cardboard king Anthony Pratt, the boss of Visy packaging and one of Australia’s richest men, published in the Herald and The Age. The Age’s veteran crime reporter, John Silvester, also won Outstanding Columnist for his regular Naked City column lifting the lid on Australia’s criminal underworld.



The Herald was nominated for a total of 20 awards, the most of any news organisation in Australia, winning five categories. Related Article Media & marketing Herald scoops young journalist prizes Herald editor Jordan Baker said she was enormously proud of the publication’s winners and finalists. “The recognition of the Herald across so many areas – sport reporting, feature writing, headlines, photography and cartoons – illustrates the depth of talent in our newsroom. “It is also a reflection of the Herald’s commitment to serving our subscribers and telling Sydney’s stories,” Baker said.



The foundation said the 2026 awards attracted a record number of entries. “It’s been another bumper year for excellent Australian journalism, and there’s no greater honour than to receive a Kennedy for your work,” Kennedy Foundation chair Carl Dumbrell said. “The Kennedy Foundation is extremely proud of its support for those endeavours that are essential to an informed and vital democracy.” Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights.
